    @zxpacr1983外媒的嘴，夺命的刀！ 盘点那些被外媒点名的习近平接班人 11月24日，中央政治局委员、上海市委书记陈吉宁落马。 去年，《金融时报》《外交事务》还在讨论他接替习近平的可能性。 翻了一下过去十四年的报道，四批名单，十五个人。 咱们看看这些曾被外界视为习近平接班人的高官，后来都怎么样了。 一、2012年，第一批接班人 美国国会研究处根据《人民日报海外版》的报道，列出了七名可能在2022年接替习近平的年轻干部。当然，有一个前提：习近平只干两届。 孙政才：49岁进入政治局，2017年落马，还被刘士余指责“阴谋篡党夺权”。2018年因受贿被判无期。总书记没当上，倒是提前领到了一个终身任期。 胡春华：同样49岁进入政治局，2017年没入常，2022年连政治局委员都没给，59岁就到政协养老去了。 苏树林：时任福建省长，2015年落马，获刑16年。 努尔·白克力：时任新疆自治区主席，2018年落马，又一个无期徒刑。 剩下三个，周强、张庆伟、陆昊，十四年过去了，连政治局的门都没进去。 二、2017年至2022年，第二批接班人 2017年，路透社、《南华早报》讨论胡春华和陈敏尔的接班前景。2022年，《华盛顿邮报》又提到了丁薛祥。 陈敏尔：习近平的浙江旧部。十九大没入常，二十大又没入常。从重庆平调天津，基本上仕途不会再有发展了。 胡春华：前面说过了，政协养老。 丁薛祥：倒是真进了常委会，还当上了常务副总理，目前仍在任。但是职位上看的清楚，这是在往总理的方向培养。 三、2025年，第三批接班人 《金融时报》发表文章，讨论习近平的接班问题，涉及五个人： 上海市委书记陈吉宁、北京市委书记尹力、中央政法委书记陈文清、北京市长殷勇，以及军工系统出身的张红文。 陈吉宁今天落马了。 张红文自2024年12月起长期未公开露面，2025年3月被证实不再担任安徽省委常委、合肥市委书记，至今未见正式落马通报。 五个人，两个已经出了状况。 四、2026年，第四批接班人 11月6日，美国《外交政策》又提到了一个人：1972年出生的新任上海市长朱忠明，外界一度猜测他可能被培养为习近平的接班人。 十八天后，他的顶头上司陈吉宁落马了。 算算账，四批名单，共计15人。 四人落马，一人卸任后去向不明，五名早期人选未能进入常委会。 近年被点名且仍在重要岗位的，还有五人： 丁薛祥、尹力、陈文清、殷勇、朱忠明。 这几个人是不是瑟瑟发抖？ 这份名单还没盘点完，外媒又开始研究下一批接班人了。 难怪有人调侃：习近平这是照着外媒的名单，一个一个拿人吗？ 外媒的嘴，简直就是夺命的刀！ 再看看这十四年，接班这件事究竟发生了什么变化？ 2017年，十九大没有产生明确的接班人。 2018年3月，取消国家主席连任限制。 同年7月，习近平在全国组织工作会议上说，优秀年轻干部“不能像‘储君’一样供在那里坐等提拔”。 2022年，习近平开启第三个总书记任期。 中国古代的皇权政治有一个难题： 皇帝准备传位，太子叫储君；皇帝不准备传位，围绕太子形成的政治势力就可能被视为谋反的威胁。 如果习近平准备一直干到死呢？ 外媒研究了十四年谁来接班，却忽略了一个最基本的问题： 人家什么时候说过要交班了？ 明年就二十一大了，开会之前还会拿下哪个储君？ 拭目以待吧。

    Sharing my Op-Ed for @rapporteur_news: "The #NVIDIA affair brings #Trump and #Xi closer". The reinstatement of NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang has reinforced, rather than weakened, the US–China détente, as Donald Trump and Xi Jinping have reasons to preserve access to advanced chips. Trump needs the H200 sales policy to succeed; Xi needs NVIDIA hardware while China develops its AI capabilities. 《纽约时报》这段话没有详细的出处，周恩来秘书钱嘉东曾说周也讲过类似的话。钱知名度不高，但其女婿即是大名鼎鼎的王毅，而王在日本留下的名言是：“大使就是大家都可以使用的人。” 大使都如此可供大家使用，何况小黄乎？ 由此想起周恩来称其为“党的百科全书”的黄慕兰（1907—2017），恰好是小黄的同乡先辈，其110年的风雨人生或可给逆境中的小黄一点启示。 《黄慕兰自传》2004年出版后，即有人对这本自传的真实性提出疑问，如周恩来是否称其为“党的百科全书”；再如她第一时间发现并报告向忠发叛变，保护了中央首长的安全等等…… 对于种种质疑，出版社给出了自己的回答，2011年再版此书时对此一字未改。编者说：“2004年版《黄慕兰自传》的责任编辑梁云福老师已做了关键性的史料核实工作……不仅仅是向传主核实，而是根据传主提供的线索，到中央档案馆以及党史研究机构进行核实，在一些关键问题上作了结论性认定。” 黄慕兰，原名黄彰定，又名黄定慧、黄淑仪，湖南浏阳人，出生书香之家（其父做过谭嗣同的幕友，是留日的海归，在铁路部门任职）。她曾在长沙周南女校就读。在其自传中，黄勾勒了一生的线索：四次婚姻，四次坐牢。 黄16岁时第一次婚姻，是传统的包办婚姻。婚后对丈夫（抽鸦片、打骂丫鬟、游手好闲）不满，成为出走的娜拉； 1926年，逃到武昌，从事工人运动，很快崭露头角。黄担任杜韫章（此人后来改名为“章蕴”，担任中纪委副书记）的秘书，认识了接替茅盾出任《汉口民国日报》总编辑的宛希俨。 1927年“三八”妇女节，经董必武、瞿秋白等人撮合，宛、黄两人在武汉登报宣布结婚，婚后育有一子。1928年，儿子出生仅三天，宛便奉调前往赣西南，4个月后被杀。 1928年12月接到调令，与饶漱石同船去上海，被分配在中共书记处工作。“中央政治局开会时，我是作记录的秘书，同时还兼任党中央的机要交通员。这段时间里，党中央的实际负责人是中央政治局常委、秘书长兼组织部长周恩来同志。” 不久，黄碰到了在武汉时就已认识的中共中央委员贺昌。贺“首先提到希俨的牺牲是党的重大损失，并劝慰我不要过于悲伤，务须节哀……终于，有一天，他直率地问我：‘慕兰同志，你看，我是否有可能和希俨同志一样，和你结为革命伴侣呢？’……恩来说：‘很好，贺昌同志是值得你爱的，我同意你们结合。’就这样，我们经组织上的批准，也没举行什么结婚仪式，就在旅馆里共同生活了。” 1931年中共中央委员关向应被捕，但是并未暴露身份。周恩来十分着急，令陈赓设法将关向应营救出来。 组织安排黄住进一个单线联系点。“一个白俄公寓，三十块钱一个月的房租，连同伙食在内一个月要付八十多元……打扮成一位上层妇女，我烫了头发，穿上半高跟鞋，戚元德还给我做了一件乔其纱旗袍，光是这件旗袍就花了好几十元……这一切都布置停当后，我正式开始了营救工作。” 第一条要钓的鱼是陈志皋，陈是律师，而且陈父在上海具有极大影响力。“贺昌临行前，来向我辞行话别时，不巧陈志皋也来找我。我在楼上一听到陈志皋坐的小轿车喇叭和发动机的声响，就知道是他来了。我叫贺昌赶快到隔壁的卫生间去暂时避一避，我则和衣躺到床上，假装正在休息……”不知康伟、黄乐夫妇是否有类似的惊险经历？ 与陈志皋的暧昧，收获是巨大的，不但救出了关向应，还不经意之间，在第一时间得知向忠发被捕的消息，关键时刻，“救了周恩来”一命。 1935年3月，贺昌在江西会昌突围战中身亡。之后不久，黄慕兰与陈志皋结婚，并且举办了盛大的婚礼。如图2 以上的引文均来自黄的自传。有人批评黄太自我吹嘘，老茶考诸历史，发现黄并不是自我吹嘘太过，似还不够，仅举一例： 黄完全隐瞒了自己的另一任丈夫，中共党史中更为赫赫有名的人物：饶漱石。 就在前述的1928年12月黄与饶漱石同船去上海，上岸后两人就同居了。《饶漱石年谱》明确将黄慕兰列为饶的第一任妻子。景玉川《饶漱石》一书有如图3、4的记载。此书还引证了茅盾回忆1927年春他在汉口办《汉口民国日报》时的情景：“同我的宿舍隔街相对，也有一间房夜夜灯火通明。那里住着三位女同志……她们都结过婚，黄慕兰已离婚……她们都是工作有魄力、交际广、活动能力很强的女同志，而且长得也漂亮，所以在武汉三镇很出名。” 作者补充说：“此时的黄慕兰正热恋着被茅盾接替的《汉口民国日报》主笔宛希俨。宛已有妻室，但黄不管，仍坚决要和他结婚。而在此时，大文豪郭沫若也热恋着黄慕兰，他虽随北伐军在河南前线，战火纷飞，炮声隆隆，可他忘不了每天给黄慕兰发一封电报……” 黄阅人无数，所以说她是“中共百科全书”似不为过。

This is the summation of the "Chinese Americans" display at the LBJ presidential library and museum, which I visited it last week. (It was right next to the Moody Center where I attended the @TomorrowXSummit) This quote hit hard and hit home when I saw it. When LBJ signed the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965, it removed a racial quota that had favored immigrants from Europe while immigrants from Asia were effectively banned. This law amended an earlier version passed in 1952 that established the path for naturalized citizenship. Memory wafers are also binned on capacity, data transfer speed, leakage, power tolerance & other factories to determine if they end up in HiZQ or HiBM packages & capacity + data rate for those modules. The top end logic dies & memory module are used in top end SuperPoD while the next end up in air cooled Atlas-850E Cabinet. The lower end gets just 425 TFLOPS & 96 GB slower HBM & used in Atlas-650E. Atlas-950PR could also be packaged in higher end Atlas-850 or Atlas-60 product. The reduced versions in memory, data rate & L2 cache are used in Atlas-350 servers that they sell for dev boards & home users & such. Even lower ones are binned for test purposes. Key is the wide ranging performance in the logic & memory die so products are also formed in a similar way. In actual practice, it's abnormal to have a logic die w/ 36 fully functioning cubes, but didn't not pass other tolerance tests, so my guess is that fully 36 cube Ascend-950PR w/ 128 GB HiBL memory aren't that common. HW likely prices these things differently. If you are DeepSeek & work w/ HW intimately, you get even the high end 950DT for good px. If you are a nobody, then you'd have to pay a premium even for 8-card Atlas-650E server w/ 96 GB HiZQ each.

    @cnpoliwatch江西省党代会开幕，尹弘作工作报告。 尹弘在上个月的省委书记调整中，满63岁却没有卸任省委书记。他能不能升副国级，取决于他是否会在接下来几个月内卸任省委书记。 石泰峰、王东峰在2021年11月满63岁却继续担任省级党委书记之后，都在2022年4月卸任了书记职务。 如果尹弘能够撑到2027年4月甚至更晚，那么他有可能会晋升副国级；如果他接下来一、两个月内就卸任了省委书记，那么应该不会升副国级。 王伟中也是一样的逻辑。
    新任江西省委常委陈克龙和山西省副省长徐朝锋同年同月生（1976年12月），现在都是“75后”副部。两人都出身于工信部，曾经同时担任工信部的司长。徐朝锋先晋升副部级，但陈克龙先晋升省委常委。 https://x.com/cnpoliwatch/status/2047062421760532788media带图post ↗原帖 ↗
    @cnpoliwatch徐朝锋（1976.12），曾任工信部国际合作司司长，现任山西省副省长。 陈克龙（1976.12），曾任工信部原材料工业司司长、规划司司长，现任江西省景德镇市市长。 两人同年同月生，曾经同时在工信部担任司长。 徐朝锋空降地方，直接从司长升任副省长，成为全国最年轻的副省长。陈克龙空降地方，需要先从地级市市长做起（图为陈克龙简历），直到本月才获公示，拟任市委书记，但是从市委书记到副省长又不知道要等多久。当然马上要换届了，理论上最早年底可以升副部级。 央地干部交流有很多例子，但是在交流的同时，还能够从正厅级晋升副部级的情况就少得多了。因此，陈克龙的任职安排更常见，像徐朝锋这样直接升副部的，就很少见。

    @CambriaPressWhy does the People’s Liberation Army continue to study campaigns fought more than 70 years ago? The victories that secured Communist triumph in the Chinese Civil War remain central to PLA doctrine, professional military education, and strategic thought. In the forthcoming "Mao’s Finest Hour," Toshi Yoshihara examines the decisive campaigns of 1948–1949 (Liao-Shen, Huai-Hai, and Ping-Jin) and their enduring influence on how China’s military thinks about war. Drawing on extensive Chinese-language military sources, doctrinal writings, campaign histories, memoirs, and Nationalist accounts, Dr. Yoshihara traces how these victories became foundational lessons within the PLA’s institutional memory and considers their relevance to military modernization, future warfare, and a potential Taiwan contingency. Yet historical success can create blind spots as well as insights. The lessons the PLA draws from these campaigns may illuminate future conflict—or encourage dangerous analogies in a radically different strategic environment. 📚 Forthcoming from Cambria Press https://www.cambriapress.com/MaosFinestHour

    There's an interesting Zhong Sheng commentary in today's People's Daily, discussing the trilateral meeting between Trump, Xi and Putin. The commentary called the meeting "historic", but there's a very important caveat that it added: “Some international commentary has simply labelled this meeting of the three heads of state as ‘great-power co-governance’ or a ‘Yalta System 2.0’. In essence, this interpretation uses the old thinking of power politics and dividing up spheres of influence to view the new practices of interaction among major powers in the new era. This misinterpretation not only disregards the profound changes in the international configuration, but also overlooks the widespread desire of countries around the world to participate equally in global affairs. The trend towards world multipolarity is irreversible, and bloc confrontation will lead nowhere. All parties should proceed from reality, pave the way for multilateral cooperation, empower common development, and together explore the right way for major countries to get along in the new period. Only by clarifying this perspective can one truly understand the value of this meeting: it had nothing to do with a ‘deal’ among major countries, but was rather a new attempt by major countries to handle differences through dialogue rather than confrontation.” I think this is an important note of pragmatic caution that Beijing is sending, as much as it is also signalling to the so-called Global South. In essence, this is an acknowledgement that a great power compact is simply not possible, given the complexities of the world, and intertwining of their own core interests. But that does not mean that redlines cannot be communicated, crisis management systems cannot be established and there can’t be some minimum domains for cooperation or shared understanding. The question is how will all this survive continuing competition.post ↗原帖 ↗

    @BillAckmanI believe the @nvidia board is not acting in the best interest of shareholders nor in a manner consistent with their fiduciary duties. What we know is that the board fired Jensen or forced his resignation for violating company policy and/or in response to the accusation of an affair with a spy. They did so without careful consideration of the impact on the company, its customers, its shareholders or other stakeholders. They rushed to judgment without the benefit of careful due diligence or even with a basic understanding of the facts. How do we know this? We know this by how quickly Jensen was fired and how little was known at the time of his firing. It takes time to convene a board meeting. There was time, maybe, for one Zoom. And this is a decision that should have been made by a board sitting in person and carefully deliberating the facts once they are known. And they should have slept on the decision and met again the day after to discuss the facts, the risks and the other implications of their decision. The timing and lack of information did not allow for careful board deliberation. While boards can fire a CEO for an inappropriate relationship with a subordinate, it should not be an automatic decision. That is why we have boards comprised of humans and not agents. A board should consider whether or not such a relationship was consensual or whether it was an abuse of power dynamics. And a board has to consider what the impact of the firing is on all stakeholders. If I were in this board, I would not have rushed to judgment based on articles in the media. I would have made sure the board had all of the facts so it could make a careful and informed decision. Boards of Delaware companies have a duty of care which means they must make informed, prudent and good faith decisions. This clearly did not happen here. What law firm is advising this board? Or is the board even taken good legal advice? It doesn’t look like it. And now the board is compounding its failures by insisting that there is no possibility for Jensen’s return as CEO. Why is it in the best interest of the company to foreclose the possibility of Jensen’s return and to do so before all of the facts are known? This is yet another breach of their duty of care. Furthermore, the board has launched an investigation whose scope is unknown. Investigations can be extremely damaging to a company and should be carefully targeted to address whatever facts need to be known rather than be overly broad in scope. In short, this looks like a series of major governance failures by directors that panicked due to headlines in the media. They likely felt compelled to do something because they were afraid of looking bad in the media, not because it was the right thing for them company. They couldn’t stand the heat. The board’s conduct here is shocking for a company of this scale and importance to our country and the world at large, particularly at this moment in history.

    New piece with Mike Wessel: Democrats shouldn't retire the China Select Committee. They should repurpose it. A new majority should set new priorities, and Democrats can use the Select Committee to offer their own vision for China policy. We propose five areas of focus that differentiate it from what came before: 1️⃣ American domestic renewal. The Committee has previously studied what China does far more closely than what America must do to strengthen itself. 2️⃣ Avoiding a second China Shock. The wave of subsidized Chinese exports is bearing down on U.S. workers and industries alike, and requires coordinated policy steps at home and abroad, including input from labor. 3️⃣ Restoring human rights as a policy priority. Human rights have risen in importance in the Democratic party precisely as it has fallen off the agenda in executive branch China policy. The topic matters for practical policy decisions on a range of issues, including trade, technology, and investment. 4️⃣ Restoring American alliances. U.S. relationships have come under strain in the Trump administration, but they remain critical to the United States in balancing China’s scale and renewing American strength and prosperity. 5️⃣ Forging a realistic approach to cooperation and managed competition with China. The Committee has historically treated Beijing as suspect, but the hardest problems—such as artificial intelligence, climate change, and global health—cannot be solved without China. Yes, Congress has other committees. But each covers a small slice of China policy. Only the Select Committee can pull that together and balance the executive branch's dominance of the issue. As Trump meets Xi and Putin, and as the Nvidia scandal spirals, now is the wrong time to shut down the Committee but the right time to reframe it. https://www.cfr.org/articles/democrats-should-repurpose-not-retire-the-china-select-committeemedia带图post ↗原帖 ↗

And I've seen reporting that only 1% of the chips sold in Singapore remained in Singapore." [1] We will go through it slightly out of order. 1. "their Chinese sales crashed and then the Singaporean sales went through the roof." Context: Nvidia's quarterly report says: "In April 2025, the U.S. government informed us that a license is required for exports of our H20 product into the China market." [2] Now, the H20 license requirement came on April 9, 2025. [3] In 2024, H200s were the state-of-the-art Nvidia chip. [4,5] H20s were modified versions of H200s for sale in China, about 6-7-times less powerful. [6] And they were banned for sale to China in April 9, 2025. [3,7] Take a look at the figure. It is a compilation of twenty-two SEC and BIS filings and press releases. [8] You can see the fall in sales to China from $5.5b in Apr 27, 2025 to $2.8b in Jul 27, 2025 when the H20s were banned. [2,7] China was buying lots of H20s, and Nvidia then stopped selling them. [7] Nvidia's China sales crashed because they were following what the administration told them to do. [3,7] They were following the rules. Now, let's test the idea that, after China revenues fell, Singapore revenues "went through the roof", insinuating that chips were brazenly smuggled through Singapore to China to make up the shortfall and made blatantly obvious in Nvidia's financial documents. This is an outrageous thesis, based on a complete misunderstanding. The figure shows that Singapore's revenues had been steadily increasing up for two years. [8] There was no increase "through the roof" at the Jul 27, 2025 time point. The Jul 27, 2025 $10.2 billion line is the last Singapore entry we have for reasons we will see in a moment. [2,9] So, Bessent says that "their Chinese sales crashed and then the Singaporean sales went through the roof". The implication is that chips were being rerouted from China via Singapore. Yet as we have seen, the gradual increase in Singapore's sales *preceded* the China crash. [8] Bessent got the story reversed, which rules out the causal connection he stated. Nvidia also wasn't the only company with big revenues invoiced to Singapore. AMD had them too. Intel has had revenues matching those of Nvidia for decades. [10,11,12] Taiwanese chip foundry UMC's Singapore revenues are also large -- though the conversion rate of that currency to USD is at roughly NT$30 to USD. [13] Seagate has also had respectable Singapore revenue. Intel revenue by customer billing address, $ billions, fiscal year: [12] China Singapore 2023 14.9 8.6 2024 15.5 10.2 2025 12.7 9.5 AMD revenue by customer billing address, $ billions, fiscal year: [14] China Singapore 2023 3.4 2.2 2024 6.2 3.6 2025 7.8 4.3 (China includes Hong Kong.) UMC revenue, NT$ billions, calendar year: [15] Singapore China United States 2020 26.1 22.6 24.5 2021 29.1 31.2 24.3 2022 39.1 46.1 35.2 (China includes Hong Kong.) Seagate revenue by bill-from location, $ billions, fiscal year (ends about June 30): [16,17] Singapore United States 2023 3.3 3.1 2024 3.4 2.3 2025 3.8 4.4 (No China row.) For reference, here is Nvidia, this time by year, not quarter. Nvidia revenue by customer billing address, $ billions: [2,18] China Singapore Year to Jan 29, 2023 5.8 2.3 Year to Jan 28, 2024 10.3 6.8 Year to Jan 26, 2025 17.1 23.7 Six months to Jul 27, 2025 8.3 19.2 Are Intel and AMD smuggling too? UMC? Seagate? Is everyone smuggling through Singapore? No. That is not how it works. 2. "I've seen reporting that only 1% of the chips sold in Singapore remained in Singapore." This statement is so demonstrably and maddeningly wrong that it may have provoked the very financial reporting behavior that Bessent claims implicates Nvidia in having committed crimes. Likewise, Nvidia may have been so frustrated with the stupidity of people saying this that they may have changed their reporting to get them to stop. Bessent's statement also explains where he is getting his information: not from his own analysis or analysts, but from the press. "I've seen reporting". The reporting Bessent saw was so misleading that even the Singapore parliament was forced to address it. [19,20] Second Minister for Trade and Industry Dr. Tan See Leng told Singapore's parliament: "Our checks indicate that physical delivery of products sold by Nvidia to Singapore represent less than 1% of Nvidiaʼs overall revenue. These are mainly deployed in Singapore for major enterprises and the Singapore government. We understand that the remainder of Nvidiaʼs revenue billed to business entities in Singapore did not involve physical shipments into Singapore." [19] You know how when you purchase items online, you enter a billing address and a mailing address? It is like that. Minister Tan See Leng told parliament: "It is common practice for global entities to centralise the billing for procured goods and services in their hubs, but this is separate from where the products are shipped to." [20] Singapore is a trade hub, one of the major reasons being the low tax rate and costs of doing business. [21,22] Many non-Chinese companies invoice through Singapore. [23] Companies set up offices in Singapore, and they invoice purchases through those offices. [24] The vast majority of entities placing invoices from Singapore billing addresses to Nvidia did not receive those shipments into Singapore -- but elsewhere. [18,19] This is normal. U.S. Treasure Secretary Bessent should know this. It's a basic fact of international trade. Anyway, where did Nvidia send its chips, if not Singapore? Bessent would know if he had read Nvidia's SEC filings. SEC 10-Q, quarter to Apr 28, 2024, filed May 29, 2024: "Most of the shipments associated with Singapore revenue went to either the United States or Taiwan in the first quarter of fiscal year 2025. Shipments to Singapore were insignificant." [4] SEC 10-Q, quarter to Jul 28, 2024, filed Aug 28, 2024: "Most shipments associated with Singapore revenue were to locations other than Singapore and shipments to Singapore were insignificant." [25] SEC 10-Q, quarter to Oct 27, 2024, filed Nov 20, 2024: "Most shipments associated with Singapore revenue were to locations other than Singapore and shipments to Singapore were insignificant." [5] SEC 10-K, fiscal year to Jan 26, 2025, filed Feb 26, 2025: "Singapore represented 18% of fiscal year 2025 total revenue based upon customer billing location. Customers use Singapore to centralize invoicing while our products are almost always shipped elsewhere. Shipments to Singapore were less than 2% of fiscal year 2025 total revenue." [18] SEC 10-Q, quarter to Apr 27, 2025, filed May 28, 2025: "Singapore represented 20% of the first quarter of fiscal year 2026 total revenue based upon customer billing location. Customers use Singapore to centralize invoicing while our products are almost always shipped elsewhere. Over 99% of controlled Data Center compute revenue billed to Singapore was for orders from U.S.-based customers." [7] SEC 10-Q, quarter to Jul 27, 2025, filed Aug 27, 2025: "Singapore represented 22%, and 21% of the second quarter and first half of fiscal year 2026 total revenue based upon customer billing location, respectively. Customers use Singapore to centralize invoicing while our products are almost always shipped elsewhere. Over 99% of controlled Data Center compute revenue billed to Singapore was for orders from U.S.-based customers for the second quarter and first half of fiscal year 2026." [2] I am not saying that Nvidia is telling the truth in these financial statements. I cannot assess that with the information I have. What I can say with confidence that Bessent is ignorant about what they say and is clearly basing his opinion on wrong second-hand "reporting". Now, what we just saw was an excerpt from a filing from Aug 27, 2025. But it was on Nov 19, 2025 that Nvidia, as Bessent says, "stopped publishing, by the way, they stopped publishing [sic]" the Singapore figures, using that fact to insinuate that Nvidia was withholding critical information from officials in public documents. [9] But that is not what happened. As with almost everything else, Bessent is confused at best. 3. "And you can see from the Nvidia accounts — which they stopped publishing, by the way, they stopped publishing" This is the best part of Bessent's interview. If this were true -- if Nvidia withhold clear evidence of smuggling -- none would be more responsible for it than current interim CEO Colette Kress, who signed and swore to the accuracy of the documents. [9,26] This is the woman who Bessent says he does not want Jensen Huang to replace, because he is guilty of bad things. [1,27] Except she would be the one who is guilty. If Bessent were right, this would be very inconvenient for him. Fortunately for Kress, he is not. We should understand what "reporting" Bessent is reading, which forced the Singapore parliament to respond, as we discussed earlier. It is critical context. The misinformation had started by November 22, 2023, the day after Nvidia had filed a quarterly report, in The Register: "Revenue from the tiny city state of Singapore grew even faster – from $562 million in 2022 to $2.7 billion in 2023." [28,29] A headline on December 1, 2023 in CNBC amplified it: "One tiny country drove 15% of Nvidia's revenue – here's why it needs so many chips" [30] After the CNBC story, Nvidia met with Singapore reporters and answered in just 5 days: "Nvidia clarified that such country revenue figures may not reflect actual shipments." [31] From November 2023 to March 2024, I count at least 27 stories, 19 of them a misread of the filing, 4 misread with a caveat on the page, and 2 reported correctly. [32] Then we get this gem from a think tank in December 2024: "Nvidia's reported revenue from Singapore exploded in the wake of the U.S. export controls". [33] (The think tank picked its starting point: counted from the last quarter before the October 2022 controls, Singapore's billings grew 7.9-fold by late 2024, and America's grew 7.4-fold. [8,34] It then wonders whether Singapore has the electricity to run "all of the purchased chips", six months after Nvidia's filing said shipments to Singapore were insignificant.) [4,33] Then there was a lull before the story exploded again in early 2025 when China's DeepSeek's first reasoning model R1 made waves. [35] The journalist class was trying to understand how such an advanced model -- competitive at the time with OpenAI's groundbreaking o1 model -- was possible. [35] The stories exploded. I found 73 stories about Singapore's numbers from January 20 to March 2025 alone. [32] Yet even at that point, only half of the stories reported the filing correctly. The other half either ran the misleading headline with a correction or continued the full misreporting. [32] Bloomberg reported US officials asking whether DeepSeek had "bought advanced Nvidia semiconductors through third parties in Singapore". [36] House committee leaders wrote to the National Security Council on January 29: "Singapore represented 22% of Nvidia's revenue... Countries like Singapore should be subject to strict licensing requirements". [37] Yes, that's House committee leaders. The confusion was running through Congress. Nvidia responded, again, on January 29, 2025: "Our public filings report 'bill to' not 'ship to' locations of our customers." [38] But it did not matter. No matter how many times Nvidia said it, it did not matter. The seed was planted, and it would keep growing into a big, big tree. Singapore's main paper even participated, saying that the 22% "makes the Republic the biggest buyer of its chips after the US". [39] After the minister's answer in parliament, a trade site's headline ran: "Nvidia's Singapore GPU sales are 28% of its revenue, but only 1% are delivered to the country". [40] Singapore's ministers in parliament. Remember them? February 18, 2025: "This reflects the location where Nvidia's customers received the bill; it does not mean that it was shipped here". [20] I found 33 stories from April 2025 to August 2025, with similar numbers. [32] And it continued to penetrate U.S. Congress, whipping up a hysteria. Another House committee report published April 16, 2025, said Nvidia's filings "indicate that Singapore is the destination for a significant portion of its sales". [41] In that report, under a chart of the two shares, are the words: "Following the imposition of U.S. export controls on certain Nvidia chips, this trend flips." [41] That is roughly what Bessent said. But it's not true. Look at the figure in the video again. [8] Nvidia on X, April 16, 2025: "Our reported Singapore revenue indicates the billing address". [42] Nvidia's finance chief -- yes, Colette Kress who just replaced Huang as interim CEO -- on the May and August 2025 earnings calls, raising it unprompted both times. [43,44] Nvidia, at this point no doubt exhausted, told Benzinga on April 21: "The bill-to versus ship-to Singapore matter has been reported extensively." [45] It was fake news. But it reached Congress. It reached Bessent. It shaped the discussion because sharers just read the headline and ran with it. So what does Nvidia do? It switched its revenue numbers from being based on where the company billed to where the company was headquartered on its SEC 10-Q form. [9] Here is the explanation it gave. SEC 10-Q, quarter to Oct 26, 2025, filed Nov 19, 2025: "Previously, revenue by geographic area was reported based on the billing location of our customers, which often reflected a customer's centralized invoicing location, even though our products were almost always shipped elsewhere. We believe changing to revenue based upon the location of our customers' headquarters provides a better representation of the geographic profile of our revenue. Prior period information has been recast to reflect this change." [9] This eliminated the Singapore line in the table, since few companies placing orders with Nvidia were headquartered in Singapore. [9] My inference? Nvidia said something like, "We have been doing this for two years. They keep accusing us of shipping everything to Singapore. It never ends, even though we've explained it a million times. Let's just list the headquarters are the country for revenue." The new table looks like this: Nvidia revenue by billing address (through Jul 27, 2025) and customer headquarters (Oct 26, 2025 onward), $ billions, quarter ended: [8] China Singapore Apr 30, 2023 1.6 0.8 Jul 30, 2023 2.7 1.0 Oct 29, 2023 4.0 2.7 Jan 28, 2024 1.9* 2.3* Apr 28, 2024 2.5 4.0 Jul 28, 2024 3.7 5.6 Oct 27, 2024 5.4 7.7 Jan 26, 2025 5.5* 6.3* Apr 27, 2025 5.5 9.0 Jul 27, 2025 2.8 10.2 Oct 26, 2025 3.0 not listed Jan 25, 2026 3.1* not listed Apr 26, 2026 4.6 not listed Jul 26, 2026 7.9 not listed Oct 25, 2026 11.1 not listed *My subtraction of the nine-month total from the full-year total. What Nvidia did -- changing how it tracked revenue -- is not uncommon among tech companies. Here is Amkor, a semiconductor packaging and testing company, doing it in 2016. Amkor net sales, $ billions, calendar year: [46,47,48] Singapore United States 2010 0.64 0.89 2011 0.54 1.09 2012 0.45 1.14 2013 0.50 1.21 2014 0.43 1.13 2015 0.45 0.91 2016 not listed 1.62 (by customer headquarters) And here is UMC, a Taiwanese chip foundry, doing almost the same exact thing as Nvidia did, at almost the same time, with a much higher Singapore revenue. UMC revenue, NT$ billions, calendar year: [15,49,50,51] Singapore China United States 2015 18.3 11.7 12.8 2016 26.8 13.7 13.7 2017 30.8 19.0 18.2 2018 24.8 18.5 23.6 2019 24.0 19.1 20.0 2020 26.1 22.6 24.5 2021 29.1 31.2 24.3 2022 39.1 46.1 35.2 2023 not listed 27.5 59.1 (by customer headquarters) (China includes Hong Kong.) Here are a bunch of other companies that did the same thing, though they were, as far as I am aware, not shipping through Singapore. Micron, $ billions: [52,53] China United States Fiscal 2018, by ship-to location 17.4 3.6 Fiscal 2019, by customer headquarters 5.2 12.5 (China includes Hong Kong in both rows.) Texas Instruments, $ billions: [54] China United States 2021, by shipment destination 10.0 1.9 2022, by end customers' headquarters 4.8 6.6 Qorvo, $ billions: [55,56] China United States Fiscal 2019, by "sold to" address 1.75 0.48 Fiscal 2020, by customer headquarters 1.11 1.47 Qualcomm, $ billions: [57,58] China United States Fiscal 2023, by delivery location 22.4 1.3 Fiscal 2024, by customer headquarters 17.8 9.7 (China includes Hong Kong in both rows.) Furthermore, not only do we see a collapse in China revenue on Jul 27, 2025, when H20s were banned, but if you look at the corresponding China cell for any given row/date, you see a *higher* number. [8] The composite figure shows a slightly *higher* China revenue after the reporting changed, not lower, as Bessent says. [8] And what you can see is that the revenue being attributed to Singapore was re-attributed to other countries. Across the break the United States and Taiwan lines jump. Most of the Singapore revenue was re-attributed to the United States; Taiwan's rise is growth in the next quarter. [8] And the Singapore numbers are still there. They're just in "Other". They are just minuscule. [8] Conclusion Bessent accuses Nvidia of concealing their Singapore numbers to hide smuggling. [1] What Bessent really reveals is that he is infected with the mind virus, or worse. A few things might explain this. 1. The midterms were a catastrophic defeat to Republicans. [59,60] The balance of power has shifted. Some so-called China hawks who want to undermine Trump's AI policy can now more easily do that. The Democrats are clearly emboldened. Similarly, Republicans are demoralized and legitimately afraid of Democrat lawfare. AI and Silicon Valley billionaires are unpopular with the populist base of both party wings. [61] Republicans may be trying to "get ahead of the story" by scapegoating Jensen Huang. This is contemptible and cowardly. I do not know enough about Bessent specifically, but Republicans in DC are clearly drinking a new brand of koolaid. It tastes real funny. 2. We should be clear about what "promoting closed models" means in the current context. It is not a neutral activity. Anthropic is the dominant American AI company [62], and the growing cash pile from the Anthropic nonprofit network [63,64] increasingly dominates lobbying and nonprofit funding. "Promoting closed models" means promoting an increasingly influential radically progressive political and cultural influence in American life, in its most rapidly developing field. As Anthropic achieves greater success, its nonprofit network will achieve greater influence. It will displace the current legacy institutions with a broadly compatible "woke AI left". To me, there is no question that continued left-wing dominance in America's institutions in a bright red line; the Nvidia manufactured scandal, of which I am aware of no parallel, is confirmatory evidence for this opinion. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has compared China having advanced GPUs to selling North Korea nuclear weapons. [65,66,67] I believe that allowing the left to renew itself through AI and continue to assert its cultural hegemony in American institutions is an even greater existential risk than this. I do not mean to suggest by this that we must choose the binary of closed and open source in America. I mean that I find the active promotion by right-wing politicians of Anthropic's increasing dominance over American AI unconscionable. For non-ideological, strictly pragmatic GDP maximizers, this picture is still more baffling. Nvidia clearly drives more economic growth than Anthropic, yet the interests of the latter are superseding those of the former. The current policy is not even in America's economic interests. There are certain realities that we should acknowledge. 3. Smuggling of GPUs into China seems to be happening. Current estimates indicate that about a quarter of China's compute may be due to smuggled GPUs. [68] If this is true and large-scale GPU smuggling is taking place, it is not through the pathway Bessent claims. The more likely path is that the companies headquartered in Taiwan and the United States have Chinese connections, and the smuggling is happening that way and making people a lot of money. Some have suggested the forensic Blackwell fingerprints on Chinese models, suggesting that Blackwells are being trained on the best Nvidia CPUs. [69] But cloud compute, to my awareness, cannot be ruled out to account for these fingerprints. And it is ridiculous on its face to suggest that smuggling by a company of Nvidia's sophistication would be detectable through SEC filings alone. 4. If large-scale GPU smuggling is really happening, it needs to be treated with discretion. This case is an ongoing public embarrassment. If the Bessent-Rubio faction did authorize the leak, the results have been catastrophic. The Democrats are coming, and they will investigate and exploit the Nvidia "scandal" for years to come. 5. The question should be posed as to whether America is losing the compute race at current restrictions. Most estimates put America's compute advantage at at least five-fold higher than China's. [68,70] This compute gap is growing. [71,72] This makes the current hysteria all the more confusing; as Gavin Baker has pointed out, our current policy is working. [72] Furthermore, it would seem strange to have bemoaned the past half-century of globalization and the loss of American industries to Chinese imports, only to actively restrict America's economic growth in the Chinese market. The Chinese seem to agree and are, with increasing aggressiveness, restricting Nvidia's legal chip imports in order to promote the growth of domestic Chinese chip production. [6,73,74,75] There is thus a convergence of interests between the so-called China hawks and China, a development that those who advocate for an aggressive stance to export controls awkwardly ignore. Finally, I think it is reasonable to question that AI really is a national security asset on par with nuclear weapons, or even on par with any kind of military weaponry at all. Bessent is a lead negotiator with China on AI trade talks. [76,77] He was in the running for the position of AI czar. [78,79] He is one of the chief antagonists in the Rubio faction against Lutnick, trying to get stricter export controls. [80,81] He wants to regulate AI companies the way the financial system is regulated. [82] Not only did he fail to apologize for what was being done to Jensen Huang, he is continuing the mobbing by promoting yet another false narrative. Shame on him and his allies.     In today's newsletter, I talked about the controversy around the APEC dinner photograph. My take: There’s been a lot of discourse around how Donald Trump, Xi and Vladimir Putin were positioned in it: Trump next to Xi, Putin next to Peng. There is only one place next to Xi, so a choice clearly had to be made, and it isn’t surprising that the US President occupied it. Beijing isn’t coy about what power implies; in fact, I tend to find Chinese policymakers and analysts rather frank and pragmatic about these issues. And Beijing clearly values being seen as a peer of the United States. So why wouldn’t the US President occupy the priority position? The welcomes the two leaders received tell a similar story. In yesterday’s edition, I had covered that Putin’s arrival got a brief front-page report in the People's Daily, and Cai Qi greeted him on the tarmac. That was a signal of the prestige accorded to Putin, and a personal touch too, given that Cai essentially functions as Xi’s chief of staff. Trump’s arrival, by contrast, gets a front-page report today, with a picture, and Xi himself greeted Trump on the tarmac. The difference is evident. In other words, there is a clear prioritisation in the signalling, even as Beijing tries to convey its proximity to Putin. China wants to be seen as a peer of the US, not the other way around, so the highest protocol going to Trump is only to be expected. Finally, the most significant thing from a Russian perspective is not so much that Putin was second to Trump in protocol, but that he was there at all. This is the first time that Putin has attended the APEC summit in person since 2017. Western policy of isolating Russia and Putin began in 2014 after the invasion of Crimea and then after the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, this agenda became even more pronounced. But the fact that we are now seeing Putin on the stage as among the top leaders and we will see the trilateral between Trump, Xi and Putin, the policy of isolation is well and truly over.     @chinatransition政治学家吴国光在接受《中国民主季刊》采访时讲：“在中国语境中讨论公共问题有一个很大的局限，就是很多人习惯于用当政的政权所使用的词汇，也只会使用当政的政权所使用的词汇和它所界定的概念，那就是中共党国的一套说辞。比如说，一讲‘革命’就是中共的暴力革命，‘社会主义’就是中共界定的所谓社会主义，‘改革’更是这样。这当然因为有宣传、洗脑在起作用，但也是因为缺少独立的人文社会科学研究。大脑由政府来program( 编程)，当然只会用政府的语言。‘改革’这个词肯定是可以用的，但是，要认真讨论问题，我们先要对这个概念有确切的定义和理解。” 吴国光讲的情况，不但指意识形态“洗脑”造成的公共认知困境（即使反对派群体也一样无法彻底摆脱这种意识形态话术的危害），还指中共对政治话语权的垄断和操控。 前一种情况，比如很多人一提到“社会变革”就想到中共式工农革命或暴力革命，就好像非此不足以改变中国。他们并不理解，这一套暴动逻辑是一个多世纪以前的就的社会变革模式，根本无法适应现在的社会变革环境，也与同时代其他国家常见的变革潮流格格不入。 后一种情况还包括中共宣传系统（教育系统也可以看作是宣传系统的延伸）和意识形态化操作制造的话术，你接受这一套话术，就会陷入同样的认知困境，甚至不自觉也要被迫接受这套话术背后的话语主导权。这种话术特别多，常见的如“中国梦”、“人类命运共同体”、“新质生产力”、“双循环”、“自力更生”、“正能量”等等。这类话术由于其流行范围之广、影响程度之深，已经到了连反对派群体也不得不直接或间接“引用”，进而进一步扩大其影响范围的地步。这种情况意味着社会丧失了话语权，主动或被动成为宣传系统的传声筒。 社会怎样才能夺回政治话语权呢？怎样才能将极权主义污染和意识形态毒害从我们日常生活中驱逐出去呢？这是每个人都需要思考的问题。 ------ 有关我们近期对吴国光做的一个主题为《想象一个没有共产党的中国》的访谈，读者可移步至： 《中国民主季刊》2025年第3季访谈：吴国光/王天成《想象一个没有共产党的中国（上）》： https://chinademocrats.org/?p=5378 《中国民主季刊》2025年第4季访谈：吴国光/王天成《想象一个没有共产党的中国（下）》： https://chinademocrats.org/?p=5765 读者也可在此处免费下载最新出版的《中国民主季刊》2026年第1季完整版本： https://chinademocrats.org/?p=6153 欢迎订阅我们的Substack专栏： https://chinademocratictransition.substack.com/?utm_campaign=profile_chips

    @mitchpresnickOne of the more remarkable features of Washington’s China exclusion debate is the tendency of its proponents to claim a monopoly on national security concerns while dismissing those who disagree as motivated by private financial interests. It is a convenient way of avoiding the considerably more difficult exercise of comparative strategic risk analysis. The fundamental problem with this poster’s argument is that strategic risk is not absolute. It is relative. In the real world, policymakers must weigh the risks an action is intended to mitigate against the risks that action itself creates, including the second- and third-order consequences of both. This has considerably less to do with money than he seems to imagine, and considerably more to do with American industrial competitiveness, technological leadership and supply-chain security over precisely the medium and long term he references. Consider America’s extraordinary dependence on China for critical minerals, including rare earth elements such as yttrium, as well as gallium, specialized industrial inputs and processing capabilities. Some American stockpiles are reportedly dwindling, with certain supplies projected to reach critically low levels as early as Q1 2027. What is the economic and national security cost of provoking further Chinese restrictions on those supplies before America has developed viable alternatives? How does that affect America’s AI infrastructure, semiconductor manufacturing, aerospace industry and defense production? And how exactly does removing Nvidia from the Chinese technology ecosystem improve American supply-chain security if doing so simultaneously diminishes Beijing’s commercial incentive to preserve it? As for the national security risks associated with selling older-generation American compute, those risks must be assessed against China’s increasingly sophisticated domestic capabilities, including its ability to compensate for certain hardware limitations through parallel processing, clustering and architectural innovation. There is also the long-term strategic cost of accelerating the migration of Chinese developers away from American technology platforms and toward an indigenous Chinese ecosystem that will increasingly compete with American companies across global markets. We have already seen a version of this play out in telecommunications. The German automotive analogy is interesting, but it overlooks an important distinction between transferring industrial capabilities to a future competitor and maintaining technological ecosystem leadership over an existing one. I would happily entertain a serious discussion about restructuring the global trading system and diversifying industrial supply chains. But describing the world we wish we had created over the past 30 years is not a strategy for competing successfully in the world we actually inhabit today. Nor is attributing venal motives to those who recognize the constraints of that world a substitute for strategic analysis. The rare earth crisis should already have disabused Washington of the notion that exclusion can be pursued without substantial reciprocal vulnerabilities. National security is not measured solely by what the US can deny China. It must also be measured by what America remains capable of doing after China responds. The objective is to “win” the competition, not simply to deny the competitor or pretend that artistic feel good bans are a substitute for actual strategic victories. 🦉

    @mitchpresnickTen days into the Jensen Huang controversy, and the media is finally getting around to asking what restricting China’s access to older-generation Nvidia chips—whose computing capabilities China can approximate by networking domestically produced chips—could actually cost the West. Open secret - there is a tendency, among some of Washington’s China hawks, to regard business complaints about the costs of their zero-sum policies as evidence that those policies are working. Binary gonna binary. These policies are justified by national security arguments that sound super compelling in isolation, but become considerably less persuasive when weighed against the other risks and costs they impose on other important American interests. Yet that broader comparison is too often missing from the debate, sadly (and possibly, intentionally). Perhaps if government had to earn the money it spends, policymakers would be less inclined to dismiss the enormous costs their decisions impose on American businesses, supply chain security, and, in the greatest irony of all, America’s long-term competitiveness with China. Put bluntly, if any of my managers walking into my office proposing a major business policy change without providing a detailed and realistic projection of immediate and second and third level costs, there is a good chance they wouldn’t have a job when they left my office. And that is before considering the potentially far greater long-term cost to American AI competitiveness of losing Jensen Huang, one of America’s most important technology leaders. Any entrepreneur understands that the value of a founder like Huang cannot be measured simply by a company’s market capitalization. He is a one-of-one founder. His vision, judgment, and ability to build and lead an extraordinary enterprise are unique to him and can never be replaced. America became a technological superpower in no small part because it cultivated and empowered entrepreneurs like Huang. We should be asking what happens to that advantage when Washington’s approach to strategic competition can so easily come at their expense. I suppose we should be grateful that the western media has asked the question of costs at all, considering that costs and AI competitiveness are apparently no longer a high priority in America.     Trump and Xi will meet in Shenzhen Thursday. In today’s @ForeignAffairs, I argue that the so-called “detente” they struck a year ago is now under severe strain. Busan is cracking over rare earths, a new Democratic Congress will check Trump, and the Nvidia scandal is triggering new export controls. After a year of calm, we may be in for a period of tension. Beijing has used the detente to press its advantage. It is locking in its industrial leadership, coercing its neighbors, and keeping rare earth flows tight to keep the U.S. on a tight leash. Meanwhile, the U.S. has been accommodating. But Beijing is overreaching. If the United States believes Beijing will throttle rare earths no matter what it does, there is little reason for continued restraint. With the trade truce expiring January 10, time is running out for the two leaders to extend or preserve it. The meeting in Shenzhen, and the next one in Miami in December, are the last few opportunities to stabilize. -- A summary of the key points: 1) Chinese scholars see the current detente as temporary. Chen Dongxiao calls the detente a “tactical truce.” Wu Xinbo said it was “tactical stability” that is “neither sustainable nor solid.” And Shen Weizhong, a former Chinese foreign ministry official, says: “The more time we have, the better prepared we might be towards a final showdown on Taiwan or maybe another trade war.” 2) Chinese scholars believe China’s strength built the detente, not diplomacy. Wang Yong called the trade war “a tipping point in terms of strength.” Wu writes it “is not the result of the U.S. side having a change of heart or showing goodwill, but was won by China through arduous striving and struggle.” Wang Yong of Peking University calls the trade war’s outcome “a tipping point in terms of strength.” 3) Chinese scholars credit Trump personally for American conciliation. Chen Dongxiao points to his “distinct and unique decision-making style.” Zhao Minghao writes that Trump “admires power and prefers to engage with the leaders of powerful countries.” Others write he would "readily sacrifice" Taiwan. They want to lock in the current stability, as Xi declared, for three years and beyond. 4) Trump has indeed been accommodating so far. He kept tariffs on China well below the cap. He paused entity listings for the longest period since 2008. He let advanced AI chips flow to China and its Southeast Asian cutouts. And he held up arms sales to Taiwan and offered only muted support to Japan and the Philippines under Chinese pressure. 5) Beijing is pulling up the tech ladder and preparing for the next fight. New State Council orders threaten foreign firms that cut ties with Chinese partners. Exit bans keep key talent and their families in the country. Export controls on manufacturing equipment keep others from catching up. National security regulations on scientific publication protect domestic know-how. And rare-earth licenses force foreign buyers to hand over customer lists and production details, giving China a map of chokepoints. 6) Beijing is taking advantage of American conciliation to press its advantages in Asia, breaking past precedent. A China Coast Guard crew clubbed a Philippine sailor near Second Thomas Shoal. They blocked a resupply mission during Xi’s state visit to Washington, breaking a two-year agreement. Japan now faces the broadest coercion campaign in more than a decade, existentially threatening some of its manufacturers. And around Taiwan, the PLA fired rockets closer to the island than ever before. Washington has largely stood by. 7) Beijing is breaking the Busan agreement. Washington has complied with the terms of the Busan agreement, suspending the Affiliates Rule and lowering tariffs, but Beijing has throttled the supply of rare-earth minerals and magnets to the United States. U.S. officials say China has delivered only about two-thirds of what it promised, and trade data suggest the shortfall is larger still. Shortages of yttrium, used for jet engines and gas turbines, have forced some suppliers to suspend production. Chipmakers are running short of scandium. Beijing believes strength built detente, and more strength will preserve it - not backfire. 8) The way forward at Shenzhen. The two sides are unlikely to save the truce at Shenzhen. We should expect few breakthroughs on agriculture, aviation, or even AI despite the need. But the leaders should at least announce they are working to extend the truce ahead of the December meeting in Miami. If they fail, and tensions mount, there is a growing risk of runaway escalation. https://www.foreignaffairs.com/united-states/china-misreading-momentmedia带图post ↗原帖 ↗

    连茂君（1970.11）任吉林省委常委、长春市委书记。他此前担任天津市委常委、滨海新区区委书记。 长春市长顾刚（1977.04）未能顺位书记。 这并不奇怪，背后的逻辑就是卡年龄——不允许出现这么年轻的副省级市市委书记。目前，最年轻的副省级市市委书记是成都市委书记曹立军（1972.11）。 为什么卡年龄？ 副省级市市委书记，可以直升省长；省长可以升省委书记；省委书记可以进政治局；政治局委员可以升任政治局常委；政治局常委可以升任总书记。 因此，不允许有太过年轻的副省级市市委书记。 副省级市市委书记的提拔进度，已经明显比五年前更慢了。 2021年10月，崔永辉任厦门市委书记，是第一个“70后”副省级市市委书记； 2021年12月，刘捷任杭州市委书记； 2022年3月，刘强任济南市委书记。 如今，“75后”副省级市市委书记，遥遥无期。 同时，崔永辉、刘捷、刘强，都是先升任省委常委，过了几个月到几年之后，再转岗到副省级市市委书记。而现在正常履职的“75后”省委常委才六个人，其中两个上个月才到位，短期内没法动。 2007年，高广滨任长春市委书记时，43岁，是第一位“60后”副省级市市委书记； 2014年，任学锋任广州市委书记时，49岁，是第一位“65后”副省级市市委书记； 2021年，崔永辉任厦门市委书记时，51岁，是第一位“70后”副省级市市委书记； 现在，最年轻的副省级市市委书记曹立军，54岁。media带图post ↗原帖 ↗

    @CaminoTexas【美国的烂苹果，中国的金苹果】我在美国经历了克林顿、小布什、奥巴马、川普第一任、拜登、川普第二任，每个总统执政都做对了一些事，都做错了一些事。但中文世界有很多政治二极管，他们不是把政客当政客看，而是跟政客建立感情纽带，把他们支持的政客当成爹妈般的亲人，把他们反对的政客当成有杀父之仇，不共戴天。在启蒙时代，这叫政治不开化。海外中文媒体上一些反共人士，刚脱离墙内的封闭环境，不是先虚心学习，让自己开化起来，而是拿自己造反的不开化反共产党的不开化，反来反去，还是不开化。 民主选举不是选伟大领袖，而是选不是有这种毛病，就是有那种毛病的人。有位读者说：“每次选举都得在2个烂苹果中选，这样的制度还玩不玩的下去啊…” 这是一种很恰当的比喻。民主就是在烂苹果中做选择。只有中国那种没有选择的制度才会出金光闪闪的伟大领袖。从历史来看，民主的烂苹果=国民可以按自己的方式过日子。金光闪闪的极权伟人=一场接一场人祸——从大跃进、文革、独生子女政策，到集中力量发展某个产业，然后咣叽一声，连人口都断崖下坠。民主的烂苹果政客，让国民不用经历那种断崖下坠。 所以，恰恰是在烂苹果政客中做选择，民主才玩得下去。一旦选出金光闪闪的伟人来，民主才危险。一旦多数国民开始膜拜金光闪闪的伟人，民主就玩不下去了。 我在美国经历的五位总统，都是这种烂苹果，只是烂的程度不一样。他们都做对了一些事，也都做错了一些事。因为通胀、物价、南部边境失控、非法移民问题，去年大选，民主党大输。川普上台以后，南部边境和非法移民问题得到控制，现在美国人最大的不满是物价，生活成本太高。 每次选举过后，都有无数预言家出来，把事件当成趋势。怎么看这些预言家呢？他们有时候不是也能说对么？道理这样的，英语中有句谚语，就是专门针对这种预言家的。“A broken clock is right twice a day” ——“停摆的钟每天都会走对两次”。 在以前的文章中，曾经给读者介绍观察政治的一个基本方法论，就是不要被一个单独事件或一场选举牵着鼻子走，而是要看一个时间段的趋势。这需要耐心，没有足够的时间，形成不了趋势。 昨天的选举结束后，有人说民主党获得全面胜利，尤其是在弗吉尼亚，赢了很多去年川普赢过的县，说明现在的趋势是民主党会大胜。这是混淆了“波动”跟“趋势”两个概念。同一个州，去年川普和共和党占优势，今年民主党占优势，这不叫“趋势”，这叫“波动”。如果哪个党接连几次选举占优势，那叫“趋势”。这是“趋势”的基本含义。一次选举一个样，这正是“波动”的含义。 这本来是生活常识，也是语文用词的常识，但党国教育不但摧毁正常人的常识，也打乱正常的语文用词。语言是思考的工具，语文用词混乱，思维肯定混乱。从这种教育出来的人，需要付出很大努力，恢复常识，才能看到现实。 在中文世界，有两伙人比较反常识，在认知方面都打着党国的烙印。一伙叫小粉红，一伙叫川粉。 小粉红和川粉有个共同特点，就是攻击英文主流媒体。他们大部分没有阅读英文媒体的能力。任何行业都会存在问题，媒体也不例外。虽然媒体会有倾向性，但到目前为止，英文世界最可靠的新闻来源仍然是主流媒体。小粉红和川粉把英文主流媒体都叫“左媒”。这反映出他们的认知缺陷。 英文主流媒体，左右倾向的都有，像《华尔街日报》、福克斯新闻，都有比较明显的右翼倾向。有头脑的受众，不会全盘接受主流媒体的报导，也不会全盘否定主流媒体，更不会把一些中南海听床师和白宫听床师的自媒体当成信息来源。 虽然主流媒体有缺陷，但对普通读者来讲，仍然是最可靠的信息来源。大部分靠谱的自媒体，信息也是来自主流媒体。他们没有能力自己获取一手信息。 自媒体上谣言泛滥，信息垃圾成堆。大部分小粉红和川粉意识不到这一点，每天消费这种信息垃圾，时间久了，头脑就成了个信息垃圾筒。这两伙人整天骂主流媒体“左媒”，他们意识不到，这种行为本身等于是在告诉外界，他们的头脑是个信息垃圾筒。 党国教育阉割了他们的认知能力，把他们变成思维二级管。这些人的当务之急是恢复认知能力，改掉党国给他们塑造的政治二极管思维。不幸的是，只有少数人有这种意识。海外中文媒体上，不少人反共，但头脑仍然是党国给他灌输的那堆垃圾。 前几天看到，吴国光老师说：“我不喜欢反共这个词；如果要讲去共，应当从词语、概念、逻辑、观念、思维方法上去共——这是基本的建设。” 很赞赏吴老师的这个说法。他是位很有见识、很有思考、也很有观察力的学者。这些年看下来，很多海外中文媒体上反共的，只是共的反面镜像——在镜子里看，什么都是反着的，但是同一个东西，从词语、概念，到逻辑、思维，跟党国是一个模子扣出来的。中国出来的人，除非天赋奇高，即便意识到了自己头脑有问题，没有十年八年也不可能重建自己的词语、逻辑、价值观。 借用吴老师的语言，“反”太容易了，靠动物本能就够了。“去”需要能力。不幸的是，很多海外媒体上反共的中国人缺少这种能力，连这种意识都缺少。川粉现象充分说明了这一点，从他们的用词、语言习惯、表达习惯、思维方式看，跟小粉红一样，都是党国那面“红旗下的蛋”。“红旗下的蛋”，这是崔健一首歌的名字。 一位听众说，“对‘红旗下的蛋’又有了深一层的认知。以前听以为是‘The eggs under the red 我曾经在X上问：不知道为什么一些中国人对奥巴马怀有那么大仇恨？尤其是一些刚从墙内出来的，学历不算太低，收入不算太高的新移民。他们大多是奥巴马政策的受益者。曾遇到一位名校毕业的才俊，张口“奥黑”，闭口“奥黑”，这种语言，在中文网上，更是比比皆是。除了观点不同，人们看到的更是种族偏见和政治偏执。 有位嫁给美国老头的中国大妈，整天骂奥巴马，但她看病却是用奥巴马医保。如果没有奥巴马，她可能连医保都买不起。 从这些数字看，美国至少43%的人直接用政府医保，13%的人买政府补贴的奥巴马医保。中国来的第一代移民中，一大奇观就是，一些直接用免费政府医保的人，起劲骂要花钱才能买的奥巴马医保。这种精神世界堪称奇葩。 美国是世界上的财富第一大国，但它的医保制度在发达国家中也是最不公平的。奥巴马医保之前，美国几千万人，主要是在小公司工作的中产的下中产家庭，买不起医保，收入又没有低到可以用政府免费医保的程度。奥巴马医保问题成堆，但它给几千万人提供了一条出路，不至于生场大病，就要全家破产。 前段时间，有对从中国来的夫妇，丈夫在大公司工作，太太在家养孩子，两口子整天骂奥巴马医保，直到失业了，才知道他们也需要这东西。 跟克林顿、小布什、拜登、川普这几个我在美国经历的烂苹果总统一样，奥巴马有奥巴马的问题，比如说，现在左中右阵营中都有不少人批评的DEI，虽然初衷有道理，但后来严重走偏。 去年，Steven Pinker教授转贴了他自己的一段演讲，其中有这么一句：“I have nothing against diversity, equity, and inclusion. But as Voltaire said about the Holy Roman Empire: it was neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire.”——“我不反对多元、公平、包容。但跟伏尔泰对神圣罗马帝国的评价一样：既不神圣，也不罗马，更谈不上帝国。” 这可以说是对美国大学DEI政策一个恰如其分的评价。多元、公平、包容，名称金光闪闪，但实际做出来却既不多元，也不公平，更谈不上包容。很多人支持DEI，是因为支持它的初衷和目标，但发现它严重走偏以后，就不再支持了。 美国人有句俗话，“talk the talk, walk the walk”。孔子有句话，“听其言，观其行”。说的都是同样的道理。说的像西施，走出来像东施。正常人就会看着别扭。 Steven Pinker不是右翼，他有很强的自由派倾向，但他是不愿放弃常识的自由派。他这么说肯定会得罪一些已经丢掉常识的自由派。正是这类反常识的无脑自由派，去年把川普送回了白宫。 2008年，奥巴马当选总统，赢了很多相当保守的州。常识告诉人们，种族歧视在美国已经不再是从政的大问题。但一些破罐子破摔的蠢货非要反常识，用各种奇葩理论，论证黑人当选总统并不说明种族平等的巨大进步，甚至指责奥巴马能当选总统是因为他不够黑。 奥巴马8年，这些废物使足了劲折腾，2016年，终于把川普送进白宫。2020年，选民把川普赶出白宫，然后这群废物又满血复活，继续使足了劲折腾，把川普第二次送回白宫。面对失败，他们不反思自己的反常识言行，反倒骂选民愚蠢。他们跟川粉有个共同点，就是错误都是别人的，他们自己永远正确。川普选输了，川粉就传播选举舞弊的谣言，民主党选输了，一些极左分子，就骂选民愚蠢。他们虽然意识形态上针锋相对，但现实中，都是群政治巨婴。 中文世界不少人喜欢走极端。左右两边都不缺极端分子，政客在钩子上挂几个高大上标语口号当鱼饵，他们就会跳起来咬，咬住钩子，就觉得掌握了真理，登上了道德高地。他们自我感动，自我高尚化，被一些漂亮的标语口号拖着走，觉得自己道德高尚。这不是什么道德高尚，这是道德无能，没有能力面对现实中复杂的道德问题。 到中文世界社交媒体看看各种评论，就知道为什么中国折腾了100多年，连民主的毛都还没摸着了，而且在可见的将来，也不可能有什么像样的民主。即便是撞大运，天降民主，也很快会被成群结队的鸡贼玩成烂污民主。 如果人群中精神世界烂污的密度太高，不可能弄出不烂污的制度来。劣质体制加劣质文化培养劣质支持者，也培养劣质反对者。中国不是没有优秀的头脑，而是太少了，一出头就淹没在劣质头脑的汪洋大海中。 中国教育打造出无数嘴上挂镰刀的韭菜，自己明明是棵韭菜，横看竖看，都是棵韭菜，却满嘴镰刀语言，把国家利益挂嘴上。中国政治越折腾离现代文明越远，一大原因就是这种嘴上挂镰刀的韭菜密度太高。自愚自虐、无聊无趣，一代一代传下去，整个国家就成了个吹牛撒谎的骗子乐园。 有些人移民到美国，也把这种习气带到美国，时刻不忘为美国指明方向。 这几十年，在中国和在美国，从书本上学习，更重要的是在现实中，观察各种背景的中国人。有相当优秀的，从学识到性格，都相当优秀，但数量不是太多。很多人说的过去，三观大致正常。但不正常的也不少。 最不正常的就是，他们表达那点见不得人的中国特色鸡贼心思，也得挂上“为了国家好”这种旗号。有的喊“为中国好”，有的喊“为美国好”。但凡了解一点这类中国人的德性，就知道这是什么事又触动了他们的鸡贼小心思。弄这套不着调的话术，糊弄洋鬼子，糊弄青年学生，可能还好使，但见人就搬出同一套戏本糊弄，太高估自己的智商了。 有人刚来美国没多久，唐人街还没混熟，就扯着嗓子教我们怎么看奥巴马，怎么看川普，怎么看美国政治。跟幼儿园小朋友教阿姨怎么谈恋爱一样。这不是现场表演杨笠说的“普信男”么？当然，“普信”不分男女。这种”普信女”也不少。再借用崔健那首㰤，都是些“红旗下的蛋”。 去年在东京，在一个朋友聚会上，大家说起这种“普信男”“普信女”现象——他们刚从中国出来，对美国、对日本的书本知识和现实亲知都是一个一个大窟窿，但一张嘴就能为美国指明方向，为日本指明方向，就能启蒙在日本的华人，启蒙在美国的华人。 记得当时一位朋友说，这哪是“普信”，这是“蠢信”。中文世界最让人头疼的就是这群“蠢信男”“蠢信女”。先老老实实读点书，老老实实观察几年日本社会，观察几年美国社会，再给日本人、给美国人指明方向不迟。 中文世界有不少二极管：一说民主党有问题，一些民主党拉拉队就以为你是川粉，同时，一些川粉就跑来认同志。一说川普有问题，川粉的反应就像听见有人说他爹妈一样，一些民主党拉拉队就来认同志。这就是传说中那种政客容易操弄的乌合之众。 一位听众说，这是“党国给的底层代码，是标签化的思维，扣帽子文革式的攻击，这种“反”就是反智”。十分认同这位听众的说法。 我把批评二极管思维的文章贴在社区。有位听众说，他知道“非黑即白的思维要不得，但可以预见这篇文章两头都不会讨喜”。 道理这是样的，对于有写作技能的人来讲，最难的不是写作技巧，也不是主题，而是不讨好读者。一个人读书，有了鉴别力以后，会发现大部分作者都或多或少地讨好读者，媚众媚俗，中文知识分子这毛病比英文知识分子要严重，有些作者严重到扭捏作态。 做播客的道理也一样。这几年听播客，听过一些以后，还坚持听的，是那些不讨好听众的播主。讨好必定虚伪，写作技巧掩盖不住这种虚伪。 几个月前，我专门做过一期节目，讲财务自由，说一个人不用为了谋生讨好任何人的时候，就会觉得财务自由。一位听众说，中文世界很多政治二极管是讨好型人格。他们以为别人也跟他们一样，靠讨好才能谋生，写作就要讨好读者，做播客就要讨好听众。我连党国都懒得讨好，怎么会去讨好一些极左极右混球？互联网是个广阔天地，他们有他们的生态，这里显然不适合他们。 去年初，我在播客中说，今年心愿是“说想说的话，做能做的事”。说话比做事容易，唯一的要求就是不讨好任何人，包括不讨好读者，不讨好听众。做事比说话难，所以要量力而行，只选择做能做的事。写些文字，做些播客，走走路，骑骑车，每周做3次力量训练。没有理想，都是些有志之士看不上的小目标。 这几年，也越来越多地反思以前学过的理论，对自己的正面影响和负面影响，越来越体会到苏格拉底“知道自己无知”的智慧。当今世界，很多反智的，并不是没有知识的人，而是博士教授、研究生毕业、大学毕业。他们头脑中一堆上不着天下不着地的概念、理论，但丧失了观察地上现实的能力。现实不按他们的头脑运转，这些知识巨婴就喊叫“现实错了”。 理论就像地图，跟现实中的街道对不上号的时候，肯定不是街道错了。

  • 20:29 · @ryanl_hass Ryan Hass 何瑞恩
    Useful framing by @ZhaiXiang5 into why the trilateral has appeal for Beijing.post ↗原帖 ↗
    @ZhaiXiang5For 31 years, the leaders of China, the United States, and Russia have shared photographs. On November 19, they will finally share a negotiating table of their own. And it will happen in China. Following announcements by the United States and Russia over the weekend, China's Foreign Ministry announced at 9 am Beijing time on November 16 that Chinese President Xi Jinping would hold a trilateral summit with Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President @realDonaldTrump in south China's city of Shenzhen (深圳) on November 19. I spent some time going through the historical records of meetings between the leaders of these three countries. And one thing stood out to me: This appears to be the first dedicated trilateral summit between the heads of state of China, the United States, and Russia in history. And the historical journey leading to this moment is fascinating. The earliest event attended simultaneously by the presidents of China, the United States, and Russia appears to date back to May, 1995. Russia held commemorations in Moscow marking the 50th anniversary of victory in WWII. Chinese President Jiang Zemin (江泽民), US President Bill Clinton, and Russian President Boris Yeltsin attended the military parade in Red Square. In October of the same year, the three leaders gathered again in New York to commemorate the 50th anniversary of the founding of the United Nations (top right). Since then, with the development of international multilateral diplomatic mechanisms, the leaders of China, the United States, and Russia have had increasingly frequent opportunities to appear together on the world stage. In 1998, Russia officially joined APEC. However, then-President Yeltsin did not personally attend Russia's first two APEC Economic Leaders' Meetings, instead sending his premiers to represent the country. On November 15-16, 2000 (exactly 26 years ago!), Chinese President Jiang Zemin, US President @BillClinton, and Russian President Vladimir Putin all attended the eighth APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting held in Brunei (bottom left). In October of the following year, the ninth meeting was held in Shanghai (上海), bringing together Jiang, George W. Bush, and Putin (bottom right). I was still in middle school at the time, and I remember watching Jiang deliver a speech in English on live television. In 2014, China hosted the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting for the second time, with Xi, @BarackObama, and Vladimir Putin in attendance (top left). The upcoming APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting, scheduled for November 18-19 in Shenzhen, will mark the third time China has hosted the event. Since the establishment of the G20 leaders' summit mechanism in 2008, the leaders of China, the United States, and Russia have had even more opportunities to cross paths on the international stage. Yet one particularly intriguing fact stands out: Over the past three decades, the leaders of China, the United States, and Russia have appeared together in numerous group photographs, but they have never actually sat down at a negotiating table specifically set for a trilateral meeting. And the September 2000 summit of the five permanent members of the UN Security Council in New York was a five-party meeting, rather than a dedicated trilateral meeting between China, the United States, and Russia. On November 19, that changes. Why does this matter? Here is how I see it: Diplomacy: bring adversaries together. Ideas: challenge the logic of inevitable confrontation. Strategy: maintain relations without choosing sides. Institutions: turn a historic meeting into lasting dialogue. The summit's first significance is what it reveals about China's diplomatic convening power. Bringing friends together is easy. Bringing adversaries to the same table is an entirely different matter. The influence of a great power should be measured not only by whom it can deter, but also by whom it can bring together. Second, the summit offers an opportunity to challenge some of the most deeply entrenched and flawed assumptions in international relations. China has long advocated a balanced approach to justice and interests (正确义利观), a vision that fundamentally challenges traditional thinking in IR. In my view, conventional notions such as the primacy of national interests, the security dilemma, and the clash of civilizations are increasingly ill-suited to today's international landscape and serve only to generate unnecessary suspicion, hostility and conflict. This is not a new argument for me. During my time studying in the Department of Government at Cornell, I repeatedly questioned some of the fundamental assumptions underlying mainstream international relations theory. Yet I often encountered considerable resistance from a few professors and their overzealous TAs who seemed more committed to defending established intellectual paradigms than to examining their limitations. And I have always wondered: What happens when a theory designed to explain conflict becomes a prescription for producing it? One of the great tragedies of American foreign policy, in my view, is that some of its intellectual architects have become so invested in theories of competition and confrontation that they struggle to imagine a world organized around cooperation and mutual benefit. This summit will provide an important opportunity and a global platform for China to promote its vision of a new type of international relations. Whether China can encourage the world's major powers to move beyond some of their differences and seek common ground will be one of the most important aspects of this meeting to watch. New ideas about IR are not ultimately judged by how persuasive they sound in academic journals, but by whether they can help make the world a more peaceful place. Third, China does not need to undermine its relationship with one major power to demonstrate the strength of its relationship with another. Does a stronger China-Russia relationship necessarily mean a weaker China-US relationship? Does improving relations with Washington require Beijing to distance itself from Moscow? Why should China have to choose? Washington and Moscow may both hope that China will play a role in addressing certain issues, but whether Beijing will accept the agenda they seek to set remains to be seen. Fourth, perhaps the most consequential question is what happens after November 19. Will Shenzhen be remembered as a one-off diplomatic event, or as the beginning of a new mechanism preventing bloc confrontation in international politics? If the three countries can build on this meeting to establish more stable channels of communication, or even gradually institutionalize regular trilateral summits, its historical significance could extend far beyond that of a single APEC summit. Some have drawn comparisons between this meeting and the Cairo, Tehran, Yalta, and Potsdam conferences. I do not share that view. The differences in national interests, strategic disagreements, and levels of mutual trust among the three countries mean that establishing such a mechanism will be anything but easy. Moreover, no mechanism for dialogue among major powers should imply that a handful of powerful countries have the right to determine the fate of others. Its true value should lie in reducing the risk of confrontation, not in dividing the world into spheres of influence. The world is not short of great-power competition. What it lacks are mechanisms to prevent that competition from spiraling out of control. November 19 will give us another historic photograph. What happens afterward will determine its place in history.

    While all eyes are turning to Shenzhen for APEC and the possible Trump–Xi–Putin trilateral, the CPC has put out something interesting on the domestic front. Today’s People’s Daily carried the revised Regulations on the Work of Local Committees of the Communist Party of China. This is the really unsexy stuff of China-watching, but it is also the really important stuff. The regulations apply to every local Party committee and its standing committee: provincial, city and county. These committees are the real seat of power across different parts of the country. They set the direction, decide major issues, manage cadres and oversee governance, etc. The last version of this document was issued in 2015. So, what has changed in 2026? Here are four big takeaways: 1. Xi Jinping Thought has formally replaced the entire old canon. The reference to Marxism-Leninism and Mao Zedong Thought are gone. We now have Xi Jinping Thought as the guiding force. In the 2015 document, all Xi had was the need to implement the “spirit of General Secretary Xi Jinping’s series of important speeches”. Articles 3 and 4 in the revised Regulations quite clearly outline this shift, with the former specifically being basically based on Xi’s ideological propositions. Article 9 enforces Xi’s ideological and political leadership in terms of practice. 2. The changes to Article 5 in the 2026 version are important. They fundamentally expand the mandate of local Party committees. They are no longer simply in charge of “political, ideological, and organizational leadership” but rather must have “overall leadership” across “economic construction, political construction, cultural construction, social construction and ecological civilization construction” and “decisions on major issues in their region”. 3. There is now an explicit call in Article 7 to put political standards first in electing and selecting people for local committees, and stronger oversight of the people who are appointed by the higher-level committee, with an explicit reporting requirement. 4. Fourth, and this is the big takeaway, compared to the 2015 regulations, which were aimed at streamlining work and to an extent empowering local committees, this document is clearly focussed on building guardrails around what committees and individuals in leadership positions can and cannot do. The emphasis is on discipline and intensifying control by higher-level committees. You can check out all the details in my breakdown of the Regulations in the latest edition of my newsletter: https://trackingpeoplesdaily.substack.com/p/apec-preview-whats-in-the-revisedmedia带图post ↗原帖 ↗

These included real-world tasks involving grasping a Rubik’s Cube, picking up a lucky bag, and autonomously navigating around obstacles, as well as simulated tasks involving moving a basket, stacking bowls through direct control, and stacking bowls with the assistance of a world model.” According to results disclosed by the company, Astra failed to complete the Rubik’s Cube grasping task, simulated basket transport, and direct bowl stacking. The same official also said the US did not plan to raise the momentum building in Washington toward tightening export controls on companies that give Beijing access to high-end chips via smuggling or remote access. “We do not negotiate American export controls. These are national security matters that we develop in the administration and interagency process.” The official also tried to blunt any Chinese argument against tightening the controls: “The Chinese publicly have stated that they're not involved with smuggling and they are not really involved with remote access either… Us closing these loopholes should not be something that generates countermeasures… It would be it would be completely disproportionate, given their existing restrictions [on the import of US chips], [if] we close[d] a loophole to get at an issue that the Chinese themselves say that they're not doing.” Musk The officials confirmed that Elon Musk will attend. Off the record, even before the scandal, NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang was not scheduled to attend. US-China bilateral/trade A senior US official said Xi and POTUS would have an “implementation check-in, a stocktaking” ahead of the January expiry of the US-China trade truce. The official said there would be no deal announced, and continued their criticism of China’s blocking some rare earth exports: “While we are getting rare earths and derivative products from the Chinese, we're not getting them at the pace and at the level that we would like to be receiving them at… We really want to focus minds among our counterparts in China on compliance with this.” North Korea “There are no plans at all for engagement with North Korea.”

    @DavidSacksNYT has responded to my post by claiming that I’m “spreading conspiracy theories.” But which of us is the one trafficking in unsubstantiated allegations? Recent coverage (including CNN, which I QT’d) shows: — The intelligence community has not established conclusive evidence that Alice Huang knowingly acted as a spy or funneled information to Beijing. — There is internal disagreement about the strength of the evidence and whether she was recruited by the MSS. — Attorney General Todd Blanche has said on the record that the Justice Department, he, and FBI Director Patel have reached no conclusions about “who she is or is not.” — Some officials at ODNI and CIA have indicated the “Chinese spy” label is not fully accurate or is “over-torqued” based on the available intercepts and collection. — Incoming House Intelligence Chairman Jim Himes, a Democrat, said it was still unclear whether Alice Huang was a Chinese spy immediately after he was briefed. NYT’s stories (which have alleged “Chinese spy” dozens of times) have relied exclusively on anonymous officials. No official has gone on the record affirming it as established fact, and the more recent reporting reflects greater caution and disagreement inside the government. So when I point out that the spy narrative is unconfirmed and increasingly contested, that is not a conspiracy theory. It’s a growing body of evidence that indicts the NYT’s reporting.

    I joined Francesca Ghiretti on Geoeconomic Competition to discuss the recent sell-off in Chinese AI stocks. My view is that this is less about an AI bubble bursting and more about China’s involution problem. Unlike in the US, Chinese AI companies never reached such high valuations. Many went public relatively early as traditional funding sources, including local governments, state-owned enterprises and foreign investors, became increasingly constrained. The deeper issue is profitability. Chinese open-weight models have gained traction, but usage has not translated into sufficient revenues. Fierce competition and falling prices for closed models are making monetisation even harder. Uncertainty over China’s proposed technology export controls has added to market concerns. The problem is not China’s ability to innovate, but its ability to turn innovation into sustainable profits. And this raises a broader question: can AI, robotics and biotech really become China’s new growth engines when the economy continues to face structural challenges? Thanks to Francesca for the interesting discussion!     @willdepueI have a major result to share. I’ve found conclusive forensic evidence that the top 4 Chinese AI labs—DeepSeek, Moonshot, MiniMax and Ant Group—have built their newest models on NVIDIA’s most advanced Blackwell chips, which are barred from export to China. This sounds insane, but I discovered that almost every AI model carries a hidden signature of the GPU that trained it. When a model is first set up, the starting values of its weights are laid out in a pattern that depends on the exact GPU. Each combination of GPU and seed number produces a unique pattern—a sort of fingerprint of the hardware used to create the model. Traces of that pattern survive training into the published model. Again, this evidence isn’t based on any insider information or leaking. It’s based on a forensic analysis of the model weights released by the companies themselves. I searched more than six trillion combinations of chip layout and seed number and matched them to open-weights models. In doing so, I found conclusive evidence that six Chinese AI models—including DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3, and MiniMax-M3—were initialized on NVIDIA Blackwell systems. Four of the models match Grace Blackwell, the GB200 and GB300 parts in NVIDIA’s flagship liquid-cooled rack-scale systems. I then verified these results on real hardware. Running unmodified PyTorch with the seeds I’d recovered, a Blackwell B300 reproduced DeepSeek-V4-Flash’s untouched starting weights bit for bit, and a rented GB200 reproduced Kimi K3’s to a correlation of 0.999995. A Hopper H100 reproduced none of DeepSeek-V4-Flash’s, and changing the seed by one broke the match. (DeepSeek’s seed is 953049583 by the way.) The method also was verified to match 24 known open-weights models to the hardware that developers said they used. It is exceedingly unlikely that these results are a coincidence. Across six trillion combinations, the best accidental match should reach only about 8 sigma (i.e., eight standard deviations above what random chance would produce). The real matches range from 49 to 1,385 sigma, and even the weakest single test hits 20. These were data-center-scale training runs. With some analysis of release schedules and model details, I estimate that the largest, Kimi K3 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro, used 2,000 to 3,000 Blackwell GPUs each. Clusters of this size cost on the order of $150 to $200 million each to buy, and across these labs alone would add up to more than half a billion dollars of export-controlled GPUs, not counting experimental compute or otherwise. It’s quite likely that we see multi-billion dollar expenditure on export-controlled GPUs. I am highly confident in this result, and it has been independently verified by senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic. You can read the full report at http://unemploymentlabs.com/checkpoint-forensics. There is much more I’ve identified about these models through other forms of checkpoint forensics like this, and will have more to share soon.

    @willdepueI have a major result to share. I’ve found conclusive forensic evidence that the top 4 Chinese AI labs—DeepSeek, Moonshot, MiniMax and Ant Group—have built their newest models on NVIDIA’s most advanced Blackwell chips, which are barred from export to China. This sounds insane, but I discovered that almost every AI model carries a hidden signature of the GPU that trained it. When a model is first set up, the starting values of its weights are laid out in a pattern that depends on the exact GPU. Each combination of GPU and seed number produces a unique pattern—a sort of fingerprint of the hardware used to create the model. Traces of that pattern survive training into the published model. Again, this evidence isn’t based on any insider information or leaking. It’s based on a forensic analysis of the model weights released by the companies themselves. I searched more than six trillion combinations of chip layout and seed number and matched them to open-weights models. In doing so, I found conclusive evidence that six Chinese AI models—including DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3, and MiniMax-M3—were initialized on NVIDIA Blackwell systems. Four of the models match Grace Blackwell, the GB200 and GB300 parts in NVIDIA’s flagship liquid-cooled rack-scale systems. I then verified these results on real hardware. Running unmodified PyTorch with the seeds I’d recovered, a Blackwell B300 reproduced DeepSeek-V4-Flash’s untouched starting weights bit for bit, and a rented GB200 reproduced Kimi K3’s to a correlation of 0.999995. A Hopper H100 reproduced none of DeepSeek-V4-Flash’s, and changing the seed by one broke the match. (DeepSeek’s seed is 953049583 by the way.) The method also was verified to match 24 known open-weights models to the hardware that developers said they used. It is exceedingly unlikely that these results are a coincidence. Across six trillion combinations, the best accidental match should reach only about 8 sigma (i.e., eight standard deviations above what random chance would produce). The real matches range from 49 to 1,385 sigma, and even the weakest single test hits 20. These were data-center-scale training runs. With some analysis of release schedules and model details, I estimate that the largest, Kimi K3 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro, used 2,000 to 3,000 Blackwell GPUs each. Clusters of this size cost on the order of $150 to $200 million each to buy, and across these labs alone would add up to more than half a billion dollars of export-controlled GPUs, not counting experimental compute or otherwise. It’s quite likely that we see multi-billion dollar expenditure on export-controlled GPUs. I am highly confident in this result, and it has been independently verified by senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic. You can read the full report at http://unemploymentlabs.com/checkpoint-forensics. There is much more I’ve identified about these models through other forms of checkpoint forensics like this, and will have more to share soon.

    @mingchikuoKey takeaways on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation: 1. Near term, the bad news is priced in: For the stock market, this could be a one-time clearing event. Huang has now fully cut ties with Nvidia, so Congress summoning him and any follow-up investigations should have less impact on Nvidia’s stock from here. As for how Huang’s next moves might affect Nvidia, it’s too early to call before the investigation results are out. 2. Google’s TPU is likely the biggest beneficiary: With Nvidia facing succession uncertainty, Google’s TPU has a chance to win more trust from customers and the supply chain. Its key partners, MediaTek and Broadcom, could be the market’s near-term focus. 3. Succession impact shows up in 2028 at the earliest: CFO Colette Kress is now interim CEO. The formal CEO transition and the organizational changes that come with it will likely start affecting Nvidia’s product development and competitiveness in 2028 at the earliest. 4. Capacity pre-booking and spec upgrades are the key focus for supply chain checks: Huang’s product strategy pushed the supply chain hard in two ways: capacity pre-booking and spec upgrades. It’s critical to watch for any changes in capacity expansion and new tech development across the supply chain. These are among the core reasons Nvidia’s supply chain trades at high P/E multiples. 5. China demand and export controls: The share of Nvidia’s AI chip revenue that ultimately ends up with Chinese buyers may be higher than what the company has officially stated. That’s why some investors worry Nvidia’s revenue will drop sharply once the US government tightens export controls. But China’s end demand won’t disappear because of export controls. Even under tighter rules, as long as overseas resale channels exist, Chinese buyers may still pay the premium, even at several times the price, and get Nvidia chips/racks through indirect routes.
