    @GavinSBakerSomething that merits more discussion amongst those who believe it was a mistake by both the Biden and Trump administrations to allow the export of less powerful GPUs to China: Since the summer of 2025, it has increasingly been *China*, not just DC, blocking Nvidia GPUs in China. Within weeks of Secretary Lutnick saying the goal was to get Chinese developers "addicted" to the American technology stack, Beijing began pressuring its tech giants to stop buying the H20. Then it ordered them to stop buying the RTX Pro 6000D, sent customs teams to the ports to crack down on Nvidia chip imports, and barred foreign AI chips from new state-funded data centers. And as of last week, Reuters reports that roughly 600,000 H200s are sitting in Hong Kong because Beijing won't approve large-scale imports of a chip that is still better than anything China's own industry makes at scale. If allowing the export of these less powerful GPUs was a policy mistake that *advantaged* China, then why is *China* the one blocking them? From my perspective, China understands that if they are dependent on American AI hardware - either on the ground in China or accessed remotely via the wide range of southeast Asian clouds (which include SE Asian availability zones from the largest American hyperscalers) - then we have immense leverage over them in any future conflict. Being able to turn off the clouds instantly is actually the greatest leverage. Yes, Chinese AI labs still want Nvidia chips. Gray market prices for H200 servers have roughly tripled over the past year. But that is exactly the point. Beijing is willing to impose real costs on its own AI labs to avoid dependence on American GPUs, which tells you how Beijing views GPU imports: not as a gift, but as a threat to its own ambitions. Maybe, just maybe, selling China GPUs that trail our own state of the art, so that Chinese developers stay “addicted” to American GPUs and China doesn't build an alternative AI hardware ecosystem that we have no control or influence over *and* that China could share over time with our adversaries, was actually a smart, pro-American national defense policy. And letting them access southeast Asian clouds might be an even smarter policy as so easy to turn clouds off. I believed and still believed it was smart policy. And I say this as someone whose posts here are hawkish enough on China that I won't travel there anymore. And note that both the Biden and Trump administration allowed the export of less powerful GPUs to China for all of these reasons. It was only under the Trump administration that China woke up to the risk of what was actually a pretty smart, pro-national defense policy and then China began restricting GPUs. The lesson of the H20 is that a deliberately crippled chip doesn't keep China on our stack. Beijing moved against the H20 and RTX Pro 6000D as it concluded that domestic Chinese chips had caught up to them. So if China develops an alternative AI hardware ecosystem that it shares with Russia, Iran and North Korea, we will look back and think it would have been even smarter to offer China the B30A in 2025 instead of the H200s we eventually approved case-by-case. Especially given the H200 is not the frontier: with Vera Rubin now in full production, it is two generations behind what American labs are buying. All of this is to say that Jensen has been consistently lobbying for a position that was adapted by both the Biden *and* Trump admins *and* looks smarter every month that goes by as Chinese labs increasingly adapt their MoE architectures to domestic Chinese hardware. DeepSeek reportedly gave Huawei and Cambricon early access to V4 instead of Nvidia and AMD, and a Huawei-led team has since post-trained V4-Pro on Ascend chips. And if America *ever* falls behind China in AI, the China hawks here in America who helped accelerate the creation of this alternative Chinese AI hardware ecosystem will deserve a significant share of the blame.

    Bertrand: In fact, it looks like Megaspeed - Alice Huang's company - was a counter-reaction to official Chinese policy: a private sector workaround to these efforts by the Chinese government to curtail Nvidia.post ↗原帖 ↗
    @RnaudBertrandThis is the biggest irony of the whole Alice Huang / Nvidia saga: the Chinese government actually doesn't want Nvidia chips and is actively keeping them out of the country. Last year it even ordered Alibaba and ByteDance to cancel their Nvidia orders (https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2025-09-17/china-agency-orders-firms-to-stop-buying-nvidia-ai-chip-ft-says) and sent customs teams to the ports to check every advanced chip coming in (https://ng.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/nvidia-ai-chips-targeted-in-china-customs-crackdown-ft-2139111). And right now 600,000 Nvidia H200s are stuck in Hong Kong because Beijing won’t let them into the country (https://www.reuters.com/world/china/nvidia-chips-pile-up-hong-kong-china-withholds-import-approval-2026-11-05/)👇 Nvidia also explicitly frames this as a threat to its business in its latest annual report to the SEC: "The Chinese government has encouraged customers to purchase from our China-based competitors and discouraged customers from purchasing, importing, or using our data center products" (https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1045810/000104581026000021/nvda-20260125.htm). Why does China do that? Because every Nvidia chip a Chinese company buys is one that Huawei or Cambricon doesn’t sell, and domestic chips can only catch up if people actually buy them (which means money for R&D, etc.). Which means that the notion that Chinese intelligence was running honeytraps to get more Nvidia chips into China gets the whole thing exactly backwards. In fact, it looks like Megaspeed - Alice Huang's company - was a counter-reaction to official Chinese policy: a private sector workaround to these efforts by the Chinese government to curtail Nvidia. As was widely reported - including by Western media - Megaspeed built data centers in Southeast Asia and rented their computing power to Alibaba, which the New York Times called "a backdoor way of getting access" to Nvidia chips (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/06/us/politics/chinese-spy-agency-nvidia-jensen-huang.html). That is a backdoor not only - allegedly - around Washington’s export controls, but also around China's own efforts to wean its companies off Nvidia. I can’t believe the Chinese government was too thrilled about it: it'd make just about zero sense for it to run countless domestic measures to prevent Alibaba from using Nvidia chips, yet at the same time have its top spy agency help the same Alibaba get Nvidia chips through the back door in Southeast Asia 🤷 At the end of the day, as with all such stories, you always need to look at "cui bono?": who benefits? Who benefitted is pretty clear: - Nvidia itself: it's in the business of selling chips so a customer willing to spend billions of dollars on chips in Southeast Asia is a godsend. Again, as they themselves state in their SEC filings, not being able to tap into Chinese demand would have "a material and adverse impact on our business" (https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1045810/000104581026000021/nvda-20260125.htm). - Chinese companies like Alibaba: facts are, 1) Chinese chips haven't yet caught up, 2) Chinese chip companies' production capabilities are still limited and 3) Chinese tech firms' historical tech stack runs on Nvidia’s CUDA ecosystem, and rewriting years of code for Huawei chips is painful. Renting Nvidia chips in Southeast Asia is the easy way to stay competitive and serve customer demand in the meantime. - The US, according to core members of the Trump administration: back in July last year, US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick explained that the point of letting Nvidia sell more chips to China was to get Chinese developers "addicted to the American technology stack" (https://www.techradar.com/pro/china-could-move-away-from-nvidia-ai-chip-quicker-than-expected-after-brash-addiction-comments-from-us-commerce-secretary). Who does NOT benefit, according to official Chinese policy, is the Chinese state, which has made tech self-reliance one of its foremost priorities. Which means that, to believe the spy story, you have to believe that a person - Alice Huang - was effectively a spy paid by her own government while simultaneously sabotaging its tech self-reliance drive, which it has spent years and trillions of dollars on - pretty senseless. Stranger things have happened, I guess, but it doesn't pass the smell test. And there is another absolutely major contradiction in the media story. According to a Financial Times article published yesterday (https://www.ft.com/content/3238d92b-4074-478d-a7f2-d78b9e154fc7?syn-25a6b1a6=1), "a person who knows [Alice Huang] said they had been asked by MSS for information about her earlier this year after news emerged that Singapore was investigating the company in relation to chip-smuggling allegations. The agency wanted to find out more information about Huang, including the nature of her business and connections, the person said." Which raises a damn obvious question: if she were indeed an MSS asset, why on earth would the MSS need to ask the people around her who she was and the nature of her business? It's a complete contradiction with the spy story - but very much not a contradiction with what I described above: a private businesswoman running a workaround to Beijing’s own policy, which the Chinese security apparatus would naturally want to look into. Especially since, around about the same time, Shanghai police detained her business partner, reportedly her husband, in a stock manipulation case (https://www.caixinglobal.com/2026-11-10/in-depth-woman-linked-to-nvidia-ceo-has-ties-to-chinese-fund-manager-facing-criminal-scrutiny-102503139.html): also coherent with Chinese authorities looking into her network, and much harder to square with her being a prized MSS asset. And, to top it all, there is - to this day - not a shred of evidence that's been published that she is, in fact, a Chinese spy: just anonymous intelligence officials, repeated by journalists who never verified it, as I detailed here (https://x.com/RnaudBertrand/status/2119286008462381312) and here (https://x.com/RnaudBertrand/status/2120009454632788099?a=S08YXixSkS62RiilKJc&s=20) with one of the key FT journalists on this story actually admitting that he has no idea what evidence US intelligence actually has. So the claim went to print without anyone seeing the evidence, without anyone being able to check it, and without anyone knowing whether it even exists. And given everything above, from Beijing blocking the very chips she was supposedly recruited to help get into China, to the MSS asking around about her, to her partner being detained in Shanghai, my bet is that the evidence doesn’t exist at all. If anything, everything we can check points the other way.

    @GavinSBakerSomething that merits more discussion amongst those who believe it was a mistake by both the Biden and Trump administrations to allow the export of less powerful GPUs to China: Since the summer of 2025, it has increasingly been *China*, not just DC, blocking Nvidia GPUs in China. Within weeks of Secretary Lutnick saying the goal was to get Chinese developers "addicted" to the American technology stack, Beijing began pressuring its tech giants to stop buying the H20. Then it ordered them to stop buying the RTX Pro 6000D, sent customs teams to the ports to crack down on Nvidia chip imports, and barred foreign AI chips from new state-funded data centers. And as of last week, Reuters reports that roughly 600,000 H200s are sitting in Hong Kong because Beijing won't approve large-scale imports of a chip that is still better than anything China's own industry makes at scale. If allowing the export of these less powerful GPUs was a policy mistake that *advantaged* China, then why is *China* the one blocking them? From my perspective, China understands that if they are dependent on American AI hardware - either on the ground in China or accessed remotely via the wide range of southeast Asian clouds (which include SE Asian availability zones from the largest American hyperscalers) - then we have immense leverage over them in any future conflict. Being able to turn off the clouds instantly is actually the greatest leverage. Yes, Chinese AI labs still want Nvidia chips. Gray market prices for H200 servers have roughly tripled over the past year. But that is exactly the point. Beijing is willing to impose real costs on its own AI labs to avoid dependence on American GPUs, which tells you how Beijing views GPU imports: not as a gift, but as a threat to its own ambitions. Maybe, just maybe, selling China GPUs that trail our own state of the art, so that Chinese developers stay “addicted” to American GPUs and China doesn't build an alternative AI hardware ecosystem that we have no control or influence over *and* that China could share over time with our adversaries, was actually a smart, pro-American national defense policy. And letting them access southeast Asian clouds might be an even smarter policy as so easy to turn clouds off. I believed and still believed it was smart policy. And I say this as someone whose posts here are hawkish enough on China that I won't travel there anymore. And note that both the Biden and Trump administration allowed the export of less powerful GPUs to China for all of these reasons. It was only under the Trump administration that China woke up to the risk of what was actually a pretty smart, pro-national defense policy and then China began restricting GPUs. The lesson of the H20 is that a deliberately crippled chip doesn't keep China on our stack. Beijing moved against the H20 and RTX Pro 6000D as it concluded that domestic Chinese chips had caught up to them. So if China develops an alternative AI hardware ecosystem that it shares with Russia, Iran and North Korea, we will look back and think it would have been even smarter to offer China the B30A in 2025 instead of the H200s we eventually approved case-by-case. Especially given the H200 is not the frontier: with Vera Rubin now in full production, it is two generations behind what American labs are buying. All of this is to say that Jensen has been consistently lobbying for a position that was adapted by both the Biden *and* Trump admins *and* looks smarter every month that goes by as Chinese labs increasingly adapt their MoE architectures to domestic Chinese hardware. DeepSeek reportedly gave Huawei and Cambricon early access to V4 instead of Nvidia and AMD, and a Huawei-led team has since post-trained V4-Pro on Ascend chips. And if America *ever* falls behind China in AI, the China hawks here in America who helped accelerate the creation of this alternative Chinese AI hardware ecosystem will deserve a significant share of the blame.

    @BuchananBenI remember the first time I walked into the Oval Office to brief President Biden. I'd just been appointed as the White House Special Advisor for AI. The President sat behind the Resolute desk and began with a single question: "What is the worst harm that AI could enable?" I had no shortage of worries. We talked about the pace of technological progress — how, thanks to better chips and algorithms, what was cutting-edge that day would be commonplace within a couple of years. We talked about how high the ceiling on intelligence was, and about the dangers that AI would likely bring in areas like cybersecurity and bioweapons. We talked about how technology was fast and government was slow. Then he asked about the benefits. He cared about ending cancer as much as anything in the world, and AI — managed well — offers more hope for that than anything else. Most of all, we talked about what became the argument of the book my White House colleague @TantumSCollins and I have written: that democracies must lead in inventing this technology, turn that lead into a lasting advantage, and do it all without betraying their own values. Achieving all three at once will be a bitter struggle. Every choice pits security against liberty, speed against caution, power against principle. Today THE BITTER STRUGGLE is out from Crown, in hardcover, ebook, and audio. It’s our account of what happened, what’s coming, and what’s at stake. We don’t pretend the answers are easy — in some ways we’re more worried than when we started. But these questions are too important to be debated only behind closed doors, including the door to the Oval Office. We hope you will join the debate. https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/821154/the-bitter-struggle-by-ben-buchanan-and-tantum-collins/

    @ChrisRMcGuireIt is beyond inappropriate that leadership at the Department of Commerce apparently discussed an ongoing law enforcement investigation involving Megaspeed and Nvidia with Nvidia's General Counsel. It's clear that Congressional oversight is urgently needed here. To give an idea how bad this is: imagine if FBI agents were in the middle of a secret, long-running criminal investigation into a company, and FBI leadership discussed the status of that investigation with the General Counsel of the target company's primary business partner. That is no different than what apparently happened here. Law enforcement agencies (which include the Department of Commerce) cannot discuss ongoing investigations, and particularly not with companies directly or indirectly involved with cases. Everything about the way Commerce has handled Megaspeed's dealing with Nvidia is suspect. Commerce has shielded Megaspeed from regulatory action at every turn, and may have shielded Megaspeed from legal action as well. Now we know the reason why the Department of Commerce has still not blocked Megaspeed from receiving Nvidia chips: because the investigation inside Commerce into Megaspeed was halted entirely after Commerce communicated directly with Nvidia about it. And don't forget, the reason this happened is because Commerce is refusing to enforce EXISTING U.S. export controls, which would have prevented this. Current US export control regulations actually require Megaspeed, and any other non-trusted company in many countries, to get an export license from the Department of Commerce before they receive any large orders of AI chips. But Commerce publicly stated it will not enforce those regulations, and also has not bothered to replace them. Commerce could take action today to systematically solve this issue. It should: (1) immediately enforce the existing export control regulations that would require licenses for large AI chip shipments to non-trusted entities in Southeast Asia and other countries, such as Megaspeed; and (2) close obviously loopholes in controls that permit companies like Megaspeed to provide remote access of AI chips to China, or Chinese companies like Aivres (which is the US subsiary of the Entity Listed company Inspur, and provided Megaspeed with many of its Nvidia chips) to buy AI chips in the United States. Every day these loopholes persist, Congress must demand answers. Commerce's non-enforcement of export controls has metastasized into a major scandal, involving one of the largest companies in the world. Congress must prioritize this oversight, and it should be bipartisan. And Congress should immediately pass the many bipartisan bills that would tighten export controls and that are currently pending, such as the AI Overwatch Act, MATCH Act, Chip Security Act. These bills can't afford to wait, they should go today.

Second, the entire debate was about whether Beijing was compliant with Busan. You seem to concede the point Beijing is non-compliant when you write, "And yes, issues not officially part of the Busan process are at clearly at play, this is obvious to those who know where to look." Indeed, it is obvious! If Beijing is now linking Busan to items outside of Busan, it shows they are not compliant with Busan. Thank you. Third, earlier you claimed that the U.S. licensing backlog might be as existentially threatening for China's economy as the rare earth mineral and magnet throttling was for the U.S. economy. This was always dubious, and you now admit "it turns out that rare earths and magnets are more of a 'chokepoint' technology than semiconductors and SME." Exactly, so this shows you are wrong to justify Beijing's non-compliance with Busan with reference to the licensing issue, which was neither part of Busan nor proportionate. Fourth, I am glad you have also shifted your position on what caused Beijing's 2025 rare earth escalation. Now you admit that "of course the tariffs may have been a trigger" in Beijing's 2025 rare earth escalation. In your last post, and for over a year, you have suggested Biden's semiconductor export controls in 2022 were what caused Beijing's response to Trump in 2025. This was always a stretch, or perhaps a kind of motivated reasoning since you (and your clients) oppose the export controls. But you have not been able to explain why China's rare earth actions were narrow and targeted under Biden and massively disruptive and sweeping under Trump. The reason, obviously, is indefensible tariff escalation by Washington, which was at the heart of Busan. Fifth, despite conceding that tariffs were the trigger, you argue this is still all really about 2022, writing, "there is no evidence Beijing intended to play the rare earth card in serious way before October of 2022. None." This is a bold statement, dripping with confidence, but entirely bereft of evidence. Indeed, there is plenty of evidence against it. Let me list just some of it. (A) You totally ignore that in Trump's first term, China made these threats. Xi even visited a rare earth magnet maker and the People's Daily reported it and noted China's ability to strike back, saying, "don't say we didn't warn you." Again, that was in response to tariffs.     @RushDoshiPaul, thanks for the reply here. I often enjoy our exchanges, online and in-person, so please see this in that spirit. I do think much of what you have written is misleading, incomplete, or in some cases, inaccurate. To begin, a general point. You dismiss others and appeal to your own authority by stating you are "in the trenches" on this issue. By that, do you mean you're actively helping clients secure licenses from MOFCOM, as you've mentioned elsewhere? If that's the case, I do wonder whether your analysis essentially defending MOFCOM here is at all shaped (even implicitly) by your need for continued MOFCOM access. Doesn't mean you are wrong, but since you're the one who raised the point, it warrants clarification. On the substance, a few points: (1) You claim, as always, that the Chinese decision to play the rare earths card wasn't about Trump but was about Biden. But a few replies. (A) It's true China built the licensing regime over time beginning in 2020 (beginning under Trump), but it's also true they did not pull the trigger until Trump's liberation day tariffs in 2025. In fact, their April actions came two days after those tariffs, and they were in the same package as the 34% retaliatory tariff. This was about tariffs, and later, the affiliates rule. (B) Under Biden, China never threatened to cut off rare earths to the entire US or global economy. They did so *only* under Trump because he took tariffs to 145% and they were backed into corner. Even now, Beijing officials indicate it was a hard decision they made in the moment. By the way, many admit it was modeled off our sanctions and not export controls because it targeted something so fundamental. (C) It is true China took some rare earth actions in response to semiconductor controls under Biden. But you know well there is absolutely no comparison between the limited controls they took under Biden and the massive, globally disruptive ones they announced under Trump. The scale of licensing slowdown is wholly different, too. (2) I suspect the reason you keep saying China's rare earths actions in 2025 were about Biden and not Trump is because you want to undercut the case for US export controls on semiconductors. It seems like motivated reasoning since you and your clients oppose those controls. Separately, your claim that the controls don't work, which was empirically questionable earlier, is particularly thin today, when we've learned that the Chinese government ran an espionage operation against Nvidia's CEO to undercut that same policy. (3) Your framing treats the PRC's rare earth leverage as a reaction to others. Let's retire this idea. Jessica's piece, in my view and as I've argued elsewhere, is incomplete here. It is true that Beijing didn't plan weaponization in the 1980s and 1990s, but they then did so in the late 2000s ahead of its deployment against Japan. They then used it in 2010 against Japan. They even say so in primary sources. The idea that the formal regime was built beginning in 2020 doesn't detract from the idea they were already applying this tool earlier. (4) Your oddly spirited defense of China’s non-compliance at Busan rests on two claims: that “we still do not know what China agreed to do,” and that Beijing only had to issue licenses under its own regulations, meaning Busan just required it to hold off on the October controls but allowed it to keep going on the April regime. Both are questionable responses. The basic bargain was clear: China suspended its October controls in exchange for lower US tariffs and suspension of the Affiliates Rule. Interestingly, the US fact sheet also said China agreed to issue general licenses for rare earths and other critical minerals to US end users and their suppliers worldwide, and Beijing didn't deny that. You say the current case-by-case throttling is just fine, but it's contrary to a general license which would mean blanket authorization. Notably, Beijing's actions disconfirm your interpretation. Weeks after Busan, as you well know, MOFCOM began issuing a new category of general licenses to magnet makers, replacing case-by-case approvals. Why create a new licensing channel if the deal only meant returning to the post-April status quo? It's a bizarre reading to say China's April actions were totally off the table: it makes sense only if you now are trying to justify Beijing's non-compliance. (5) Nor has Beijing delivered on October. MOFCOM’s suspension of its October controls expires November 10. The US says the truce runs to January 10, but Beijing has published no extension to January 10, and we're coming up on the deadline in two days. If China considers itself bound, it should say so in writing, right? The fact it hasn't is interesting. (6) You bring up military end use, but you know (from your own clients) as well as I do that Beijing isn't just throttling military end users. You then say it's a pipe dream to go back to pre-April 2025. Perhaps, but that isn't really the point. The point is that China isn’t delivering what it agreed to at Busan. (7) I did say “US companies are not getting licenses.” But if you read the context, you'd know I didn't mean an absolute ban was in place but rather that some companies are struggling to get them, which is why export volumes are down (you and I are in fact cite the same figures here). I think you cherrypicked for a cheap shot reply and didn't look at the whole context. (8) It is odd that you claim that the US backlog of licenses justifies China violating the Busan agreement. That backlog was not part of Busan. It's quite a reach to justify Beijing's non-fulfillment of Busan by pointing to a third issue that was longstanding. (9) You disputed my claim that China's Busan non-compliance poses serious risks to the US economy while the US backlog on licenses (which is not relevant for Busan) is not existential for China's economy. You dispute it with two points, both which are dubious. (A) The first thing you do is say that the licensing backlog may in fact be existential for Chinese companies. You do not prove this, and even if it were true for some companies, the backlog does not directly target a massive segment of the entire economy like manufacturing. Put differently, the United States has no licensing block on something as elemental as rare earths. And as for your points on chips, the United States has in fact licensed billions in chip exports to China. None of this should matter though, because the licensing backlog at Commerce was not part of Busan. (B) The second claim you make, after saying China faces big threats from our licensing backlog, is to say the US *does not* face a major economic disruption from China's rare earth controls.     I’ve just finished reading William Hogeland’s book on Hamilton. As a hard-core admirer of Hamilton since the early 1990s, and someone who has long regarded him as the greatest of the Founding Fathers, I think it is a brilliant book, even though Hogeland sets out quite deliberately to demolish Hamilton’s highly romanticized current reputation. He shows that Hamilton’s ambitions were not particularly democratic, although I suspect many of us already knew that, and had long thought that, for all his genius, or perhaps precisely because of it, he would have made a dangerous president who would have undermined democratic institutions. Nonetheless, the book confirms, even more than many of the more favorable accounts, just how brilliant, far-seeing, and hard-working a figure he was. In a way, it is also a very good explanation of why democracy is simultaneously so grubby and yet the best of all political systems. It is built around institutional adjustment, a system that may seem messy but that. effectively prevents any one individual or group from taking the country too far in any direction. Democracy may not be especially efficient in the short term, but it is incredibly efficient in the long term. Even a genius like Hamilton, with his extraordinary gifts, ferocious energy, powerful allies, and formidable reputation, could not take the country too far down a dangerous road. Other countries could learn from that. The book has also greatly increased my interest in Albert Gallatin, the great opponent of Hamilton, whose statue in front of the US Treasury I have always resented. In Hogeland’s telling, he turns out to have been a great builder and rather like Hamilton himself. P.S. Interesting trivia. It seems that the body of Charles Atlas was the model for both Hamilton's statue and Gallatin's statue.media带图post ↗原帖 ↗

    @pstAsiatechYes, lets indeed worth correcting the scene here, as this is too important issue in US China relations to be mischaracterized. The perspective here is from someone in the trenches on the issues on a day to day basis, rather than from people who are assessing at a healthy distance, and may not appreciate the nuance of the situation. First. The Chinese export control licensing regime announced in April 2025 was not a response to the tariffs. As Jessice Chen Weiss and Gloria Xiong lay out brilliantly in the FA piece, the critical minerals controls started in the Biden administration, and really only in earnest in response to the October 2022 US export controls. https://www.foreignaffairs.com/china/how-china-found-most-potent-weapon-xiong-weiss For people who talk to Chinese officials regularly, the answer was even more clear that the rare earths were a direct, and of course delayed, response to the complexity and sweeping nature of the US controls in 2022, 2023, and 2024. It took MOFCOM and other Chinese ministries time to gain control of a fractious and complex industry of suppliers and traders. One Chinese official commenting in 2026 noted that China’s addition licensing requirements rolled out in October 2025, were the key piece in “China’s full response to the October 2022 US controls.” So anyone trying to still argue that the Trump tariffs were the cause of Chinese rare earths regime is simply engaging in wishful thinking. The facts on the ground tell another story. In any case, no country could have even an incomplete licensing regime in place after just a few days, so the planning and preparation, including controls on gallium, germanium, graphite, indium, and other critical minerals well predates April 2025. Second, “China was supposed to let rare earths flow, and they have not” is a fairly wildly inaccurate characterization of the reality on the ground. We still do not know exactly what China agreed to do, there was not statement from the Chinese side specific to rare earth licensing. What we know, again, from first had experience and not unsubstantiated conjecture, is that Beijing agreed to issue licenses, as the US does on controlled items, according to China’s export controls regulations. These regulations state that exports of rare earths and magnets are prohibited for military and defense industrial end use. So, China was not “supposed to” do anything, other than abide by its own regulations. The idea that the situation would go back to what held prior to April 2025 is a pipedream, and the fact that people continue to assert this shows how out of tough with reality they remain. “US companies are not getting licenses.” This may be the most patently inaccurate of assertions here. Even USTR Greer and Treasury Secretary Bessent acknowledge that roughly 2/3 of licenses are being issued. I know personally of dozens of licenses for critical components and materials issued by MOFCOM just over the past month. MOFCOM has not issued guidance formally extending the suspension of its October 2025 rare earth controls. Until last Thursday, the Commerce Department had not issued a formal Federal Register notice of the extension of its suspension of the Affiliates Rule. Important context. Third, the reason many people, not just Kyle, in industry rightly raise the issue of the massive backlog of BIS licenses that have not been issued to US companies, is that it seems rather strange to be criticizing MOFCOM for its licensing process, which is just as much, or more complex than that of BIS, and ignoring the licensing process in Washington. Of course these are not part of the formal process, but the are part of what every company impacted by licensing delays experiences, and some US companies are on both ends of these delays. Hence from an industry point of view, the US government should be raising these licensing issues in the context of asking about China’s licensing process. More important context. Fourth, how does a former US government official know that “the licensing queue…is not existential for Chinese companies? Talk to any of them recently? The licencing queue, coupled with other existing controls, which many believe have produced more damage to US companies than any national security gain, are in fact existential to Chinese companies, and further controls, such as the MATCH Act, are clearly so. But understanding the linkages here is critical, and it is this broader context that matters here. “But rare earths access is a gun to the head of the entire US economy.” Wow, quite the hyperbole. Understanding how wrong this is would be complex and take some time to explain, and also requires understanding of multiple complex supply chains. First of all, a licensing regime is just that, a licensing regime. Were the US controls in October 2022 “a gun to the head of the entire Chinese economy?” One could make an argument that they were, even more so than with rare earths and the US economy. China responded with the rare earth controls, suggesting that the US controls were pretty serious. “The entire economy”” Well, first of all, as noted, the vast majority of licenses are being issued, things are not as easy as they were before the licensing regime, but licenses are being issued, so no, not the “entire economy.” Hint, much of the US economy is services, not advanced manufacturing. What would be more accurate is to say that there are no licenses being given for rare earths and magnets for military and defense industrial end use. Just as the US is controlling semiconductors with potential military end uses. This is what great powers do. So what does this all mean? Yes, without real understanding in Washington that Beijing can and will respond to any escalation, and wants to see the Busan truce extended until the end of the Trump administration, we are in a world where the relationship will not be very stable, strategic, let alone constructive. But lets be clear about the causes of the situation, once you start weaponizing supply chains without a clear understanding of the potential consequences, you have to live with the consequences. Here we are. Note: implementation of the Affiliates Rule and China's October 2025 controls and rare earths and magnets would be catastrophic for global supply chains. Here is the real gun held to the head of the global economy. So why don't both sides rescind the rules completely? That would show real strategic thinking. End Thread.

    This raises an interesting question. The Trump administration feels Beijing has not fulfilled the Busan agreement. Others disagree. So who is right? And what does this mean for the next few months and for next year? It's worth first setting the scene. The Trump administration erred in starting a trade war, taking tariffs on China to 140%, and then folding abruptly when Beijing retaliated with rare earths. That resulted in the Busan deal with Beijing last year. But it implementation is mixed. First, the United States was supposed to suspend the affiliates rule and lower tariffs, and it did. The affiliates rule remains suspended, and on tariffs, as @Brad_Setser notes, "the U.S. has actually over delivered on its Busan commitments (the term 2 tariffs fell to 12.5%, well below the 20% cap)." SCOTUS played a role, of course. Second, China was supposed to let rare earths flow, and they have not. The administration claims, and data indicates, that those flows are below what they should be by 30-50%. U.S. companies are not getting licenses. US consultancies and trade associations are trying to help them navigate MOFCOM. What's more, the "truce" was extended to January 10, and as far as I can tell MOFCOM hasn't issued a guidance formally extending the suspension date of its rare earth controls. Third, the items Kyle (and others ) raise aren't part of the deal. Clearing the BIS license queue was never part of Busan, and even so, the US did license H200 exports. Implementation of the 30-for-30 tariff cuts are not part of Busan either, and they were designed to take effect after going through domestic processes, by MOFCOM's own admission. Fourth, there is a lack of proportionality here, too. The licensing queue and thirty-for-thirty deal are not existential for Chinese companies. But rare earths access is a gun to the head of the entire US economy. So what does all this mean? In November, Trump and Xi will have an awkward meeting in Shenzhen. In December, they'll have an awkward meeting in Miami. And then in January, they won't have any meetings. The truce will expire on January 10th. Barring an extension at one of the upcoming summits, we are looking at a period of possible economic tension and escalation in January without a summit on the horizon to put the brakes on a spiral. So if 2026 was the year of so-called detente, 2027 may bring something different. I don't think this is priced in by analysts or the markets.post ↗原帖 ↗

    It is true that spending on goods and services creates nominal income, but it increases aggregate real income only to the extent that it leads to an expansion in real production. It is also true, as an accounting identity, that a government deficit has a counterpart in a net financial surplus outside government, but the identity tells us nothing about the direction of causation. The causal relationship can run in either direction, and the two can reinforce one another. Finally, although many MMTers are emphatic about the first four propositions, they too often forget the fifth, which may be the most important.post ↗原帖 ↗
    @foscaeconJust remember: 1. Spending creates income. 2. Loans create deposits. 3. Taxes do not fund spending. 4. Government deficits create non-government financial surpluses. 5. Real resources, not money, constrain sovereign government spending.

    @petereharrellA few ideas on trade and economic security for the new Democratic congress: 1. Legislate no new tariffs on North America without Congress's approval. Repeal 338 and prohibit new uses of 301 and 232 within North America. Trump should still renegotiate USMCA and bring a new deal to Congress to address rules of origin, etc. Given USMCA passed 89-10 in the Senate and 385-41 in the House, there should be bipartisan support for this. (AD/CVD tariffs would still apply). 2. Pass a bill excluding various price-sensitive consumer goods (coffee, etc.) from U.S. 301 tariffs. 3. Pass--but amend--the Remote Access Security Act to limit foreign access to U.S. compute, but carve in companies based in NATO allies so that the Act doesn't end up being used against close U.S. friends and partners. 4. Codify chip export controls on China and close loopholes, including the loophole that allows sales of AI chips to China in exchange for a rev-share with the U.S. government. Over the longer term the U.S. needs to do a deep rethink of its trade and tariff statutes (e.g., make safeguards more flexible and useful and expand AD/CVD duties, while adding more oversight to 232 and 301). But that is probably not a Q1 2027 project, whereas I think the four ideas above could be....

This policy establishes a new, government-wide screening requirements for synthetic DNA and the equipment used to make it.     One of my favorite examples of Chinese tech spillovers: China doesn’t just make solar panels. It makes solar manufacturing equipment too, including equipment for slicing silicon wafers. This wafer-slicing equipment typically uses diamond-coated wires. China also has the world’s largest synthetic diamond industry. These capabilities also benefit China's silicon carbide (SiC) industry. SiC is one of the hardest industrial materials and requires specialized cutting equipment, often using diamond abrasives. Chinese companies like Gaoce have expanded from solar wafer-cutting equipment into SiC semiconductor manufacturing equipment. SiC semiconductors are increasingly important in power electronics, particularly EVs, high-power industrial motor drives, and emerging solid-state transformers. Solid-state transformers are a promising technology for managing complex power grids, especially those with lots of clean energy. As well as AI data centers. (And now China is considering placing export controls on some of this solar manufacturing equipment)media带图post ↗原帖 ↗

Codify chip export controls on China and close loopholes, including the loophole that allows sales of AI chips to China in exchange for a rev-share with the U.S. government. Over the longer term the U.S. needs to do a deep rethink of its trade and tariff statutes (e.g., make safeguards more flexible and useful and expand AD/CVD duties, while adding more oversight to 232 and 301). But that is probably not a Q1 2027 project, whereas I think the four ideas above could be....

    @JDVanceOne of the things the data analysts on our side obsessed over was "composition"—whether the electorate looked close enough to 2024 for Republicans to win. And despite polls that showed a Democrat blowout, the data kept on telling us the same story: in some states turnout was merely OK, in other states it was downright amazing, and in no state was it catastrophic. There was a genuine sense of optimism on our team: our people were showing up. So, I asked the smartest data guy I know, does that mean we're going to shock the world? "No," he told me. "We might do better than the polls suggest. But the data is telling us that a lot of Trump/Vance 2024 voters are pissed and planning to vote for the other guys. Our voters are turning out, but they may not vote for us." Well, that looks prophetic now. Our voters did show up. In Florida, for example, the electorate was 9 points more Republican than Democrat, just a couple points worse than 2024. Undoubtedly there were places we could have done better on turnout. But the main problem is not turnout. The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026. There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why that is. One of the pollsters I really respect told me that our economic messaging wasn’t sharp enough down the stretch. I’m sure that’s true. But the real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone. Another pollster—one of the smartest people I know in politics, told me yesterday we’d lose the generic ballot by 13 points. I felt negative going into Tuesday, but even I was shocked by this. In his polling, he saw that a lot of Trump 2024 voters were angry and planning to vote for Democrats. He asked those voters who had abandoned us what would cause them to come back on our team. The top four answers, accounting for nearly all of the responses were: 1) End the war 2) Focus on cost of living/inflation 3) Put America First 4) Change our relationship to Israel Our voters showed up. And the above four reasons are why many of them voted for Democrats. This is according to a pollster who nailed the results. While many spent Monday attacking Rachel Campos Duffy for calling for a diplomatic resolution to the conflict, it turns out her political advice was sound. (She’s also a great person.) In the next few months, there's going to be a lot of gaslighting. Expect to hear any number of establishment politicians say the solution to our woes is amnesty. I'm open to the idea that we should change enforcement—by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance. But anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you. The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night. If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest. But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there. I remain hopeful about our country. To the people who are pissed off and want to say, “I told you so”: you’re right, you did tell us so. Take that energy into electing Republicans who share your worldview.     Sharing a report that I co-authored with Rajeswari Sengupta on "#India in the eye of the storm: How to read the rupee weakness". Few large economies are as exposed to the Iran war as India. It imports nearly 90 percent of its oil and most of its cooking gas, much of it through the Strait of Hormuz, and the Gulf is a key trading partner and home to millions of Indian workers. The war has hit through several channels: a much higher energy bill, pressure on food and fertiliser prices, costlier shipping and a widening current account deficit. Growth has held up so far, but inflation is rising and the Reserve Bank has switched from easing to tightening. The Indian rupee has been steadily depreciating since the war began but the war is not the only factor responsible for the rupee’s fall. It was a stress test that exposed a problem years in the making. The rupee was already sliding in 2025, while growth was the fastest of any major economy and inflation close to zero. Strong fundamentals should lift a currency. In India, the opposite happened. The reason lies in the capital account. The external deficit is modest, but India no longer attracts enough durable foreign capital to pay for it. Foreign direct investment has largely bypassed India for East Asia, and much of what arrives soon leaves again. Portfolio flows fill the gap, and they leave precisely when most needed. For investors, the key is to separate the cyclical from the structural. Part of the outflow reflects an expensive equity market that has deflated and a global rush into the AI trade, where India offers little exposure. That part can reverse. The rest reflects an economy that produces too little of what it needs and exports too little of what it produces. The Reserve Bank’s response has bought time but not changed this picture. Heavy FX intervention, curbs on currency derivatives markets and an emergency deposit scheme have avoided a disorderly collapse, but raised hedging costs, reduced the reserve buffer and signalled anxiety to markets. Our recommendation is therefore to let the adjustment run its course. Once Indian assets become sufficiently cheaper, a rebound may come, but a cyclical bounce would not fix the underlying weakness. The time to invest is when the government moves on the reforms we set out: letting the rupee float freely, restoring credible protection for foreign investors, cutting input tariffs, implementing the trade agreements it signed and accelerating electrification to cut energy imports. That would strengthen the rupee for the right reasons and mark a genuine entry point. http://research.natixis.com/Site/en/publication/-y7JOfj1Z9KrOBnkbnjmGw%3D%3D?from=sharepost ↗原帖 ↗

    Sharing a report that I co-authored with Rajeswari Sengupta on "The Missed Opportunity in US – India Relations and Who Will Benefit?". Under Trump 1.0, #India rose to become one of Washington’s closest strategic partners: new defence agreements, a revived Quad and an Indo-Pacific strategy with India at its centre. Trade was the Achilles’ heel – India lost its #US trade preferences in 2019 and a limited deal never materialised – but the personal bond between Modi and Trump held the relationship together. The Biden years institutionalised it further, through cooperation on critical technologies, the co-production of US jet engines in India and regular Quad summits, while setting trade aside and tolerating India’s purchases of Russian oil for the sake of the China agenda. Biden’s pragmatism had limits: an alleged Indian plot to murder a Sikh separatist on US soil soured his final year. Trump 2.0 has been different in kind, not degree. Between February 2025 and October 2026 India went from a celebrated “MEGA partnership” to the highest US tariff rate in Asia, 50 percent, and then back to a 10 percent duty, below most competitors – still without a signed trade agreement. The personal rapport that once anchored the relationship now amplifies its swings: Trump’s claim to have brokered the India–Pakistan ceasefire and the “dead economy” slur did as much damage as any tariff. The defining feature of US–India relations is no longer their direction but their volatility. Three takeaways stand out. First, India keeps holding hands with the United States: defence co-production and technology cooperation, including a US-led alliance on chip supply chains, survived the tariff war, and Washington’s strongest lever is now access to AI, not tariffs. Second, India is increasingly flirting with China: flights, visas and border trade are back, curbs on Chinese investment have been eased and Xi Jinping came to New Delhi for the BRICS summit. Third, Europe’s gains look less secure than the January 2026 “mother of all deals” suggested: the free trade agreement is unsigned and the second phase – on procurement and investment protection – is stuck. If Washington’s erratic treatment of India continues, the logical end point could be an India much closer to China, leading a Global South coalition rather than becoming the independent pole Europe hopes for. Yet this is not settled: the US mid-term elections on 3 November could restrain or embolden Trump’s transactionalism, and with it India’s choices. http://research.natixis.com/Site/en/publication/hCOqUz4-DZKf-mJOK_algw%3D%3D?from=sharepost ↗原帖 ↗

    谢谢！post ↗原帖 ↗
    @lanquqing《走向共产党之后的中国：转型八论》（Towards a Post-Communist China: Eight Treatises on Transformation），2024年由博登书屋出版，共三卷、逾百万字。它不是单一主题的专著，而是把作者多年来的学术文章、时评和访谈汇编成八辑，核心是回望中国从改革开放到“逆转型”的路径，剖析当前制度，并探讨走向后共产党时代的可能。 作者背景与核心主张 吴国光是斯坦福大学中国经济与制度研究中心高级研究员。1980年代他曾在赵紫阳政治体制改革研讨小组工作，参与起草十三大报告相关部分，是体制内改革的亲历者。1989年前后赴美，此后长期以学术方式研究中共制度与转型。 书的主线可以概括为几点： “逆转型”诊断：习近平时代不是简单延续邓、江、胡，而是从“威权+市场”向更强的极权回摆（2018年修宪是关键节点）。市场化带来的社会多元被视作对一党垄断的威胁，因此要收紧控制。1989年镇压本身就是一次逆转型，之后经济补救形成了所谓“中国模式”，但政治改革基本终结。 制度不可持续：共产党制度（一党垄断权力的规则）在全球已垮台30多年，历史证明其弊病与不可持续性。中共制度与民众利益、与可持续繁荣之间存在根本矛盾。真正民主化必须以结束这种垄断为前提，而不是在党内微调或只换领导人。 路径：民变促发官变：自上而下改革已无可能。可能的突破是基层或社会层面的民变扩大，导致镇压失效、精英内部出现分歧，最终促发制度变化。他并不主张简单“消灭共产党”，而是改变游戏规则——允许竞争性选举，如果共产党在自由选举中获胜仍可执政。 替代图景：很多人无法想象没有中共的中国，总觉得会乱、会分裂。吴强调需要提供另一种制度安排的具体图景：权力受制约、权利受保障、基层自治传统可被重新激活（例如疫情初期一些地方的自保现象）。他还提出过“县政中国”等务实设想（县级司法独立、媒体自由、直选等）。 全书分八辑，涵盖1989天安门、赵紫阳改革、中国模式、党代会制度、习近平新时代、政治转型路径、历史经验、文化重建等。 吴国光这本书的视角正好提供了一个制度层面的对照：在当前一党垄断、不断收紧控制的体系下，数字人民币这类工具更容易被用来强化监控、条件化资金使用和实时干预，与“逆转型”逻辑相符。后共产党时代如果真能建立权力制约与权利保障的制度，这类全面可追踪、可编程的央行货币受到的制度约束会强得多。 当然，这是吴基于自己的制度分析和历史经验提出的论点，不是预言。他强调要让人看见“没有中共的中国会是什么样子”，而不是只停留在批判。

    @ChrisRMcGuireIt is so frustrating and short-sighted that we haven’t updated export controls to stop this. This loophole has been reported for years. Commerce controls high bandwidth memory chips in 3A090.c. But unlike for AI chips, it does not have a corresponding control in 4A090 that also controls items that CONTAIN a high-bandwidth memory chip. This is why a high-bandwidth memory chip in isolation is controlled, but a chip soldered to a board is not. This makes no sense. The fix here is easy: add a new control to 4A090.c that reads, “c. Computers, "electronic assemblies," and "components" containing integrated circuits, any of which meets or exceeds the limits in 3A090.c.” That’s it, problem solved. All shipments of items that contain high-bandwidth memory chips would require a license. Also, if Commerce actually takes that advice, at the same time it should also update the regs so that 3A090.a and 4A090.a also include the memory bandwidth and interconnect parameters that Commerce has privately subjected Nvidia, AMD, and others to since April 2025, but has never made public. Putting these requirements into public regulations and making them applicable to every company could have helped stop some of this smuggling. It’s also very basic good governance, as export controls should wherever possible be transparent and applied uniformly, not private and applied only on certain companies. This is yet another consequence of Commerce not taking export controls seriously. The next time BIS claims they are doing more on export control enforcement than ever, remember this story, the Megaspeed fiasco, and the many others like them that are published every week. Export control enforcement has never been worse.

    @YashengHuangThe Rise of the China Model A widespread notion is that China’s impressive growth was because of “the China Model”—statist finance, massive infrastructural investments, and industrial policy. Yes, the China Model produced impressive GDP growth but in the 1980s, the growth model then—which I call “the directionally-liberal model”—produced equally robust GDP growth, plus comparable household income growth and an economy dependent on domestic consumption. Gini fell and it stayed at a level typical of other East Asian economies. A fundamental feature of this model is that it was pro-rural and because rural economy was more market-driven, a pro-rural orientation was also more pro-market, and pro-people when 70 to 80 percent of the population was rural. In the 1990s, the leadership pivoted away from this model, to a more pro-urban China Model, which is familiar to observers of China. I would venture that the many have very little knowledge of: 1) that a directionally-liberal model ever existed, 2) that it produced the kind of benefits to the Chinese households proportional to the GDP growth, and 3) that there was this consequential pivot in the 1990s that fundamentally changed the nature of the Chinese growth. The goal of my 2026 book is to set the record straight and since the publication of this book, I have now been working on a book project that will present even more detailed data and evidence about this consequential policy pivot and about the long-term economic consequences of this policy pivot. The topics that occupy the current narratives about China, overcapacity, across-the-board export surge, and anemic domestic consumption, can all be traced to their root—this shift in the 1990s from a pro-rural growth model to one that is more pro-urban. Stay tuned. Below is Part 3 of Chapter 1 of my book, Statism with Chinese Characteristics. Part 1 and Part 2 were published in my previous Substack posts. https://yashenghuang.substack.com/p/the-rise-of-the-china-model?r=16uub&utm_campaign=post-expanded-share&utm_medium=web
